title: "Multi-year temporal deep learning and open satellite data lower the detectability floor for low-severity spruce beetle mortality in Southcentral Alaska"

abstract: |
  Spruce beetle (*Dendroctonus rufipennis*) has killed spruce across
  Southcentral Alaska since about 2016, yet roughly ninety per cent of the
  mortality sits in stands of areal severity below 0.05, beneath the detection
  floor of Landsat change analysis, and the aerial survey record understates
  this dispersed damage. Few studies have asked whether the temporal dimension
  of freely available satellite data reaches below that floor, and none has
  asked it of a spruce beetle outbreak in Alaska with radar, which cloud does
  not stop. This study tests whether temporal deep learning on a monthly
  Sentinel-1 radar series lowers the floor, across 160 stand blocks sampled
  over the Southcentral outbreak region and assigned wholly to eight spatial
  cross-validation folds. Terrain-flattened dual-polarisation backscatter from
  one satellite track, speckle-filtered across the length of the series and
  held at 30 m, supplies monthly sums and differences of the two polarisations
  from June 2017 to the present, with climate variables defined from the
  beetle's biology fitted at the same monthly step, to a temporal convolutional
  network and a Transformer encoder trained on dead-spruce crowns digitised
  from statewide sub-metre image mosaics of 2020 and 2023; comparison of the
  two epochs supplies interval-censored mortality-onset labels and a
  cross-epoch consistency check on the labels themselves. Skill is reported per
  severity stratum under block cross-validation against the published
  shortwave-infrared floor, and evaluated independently against a
  high-resolution severity product whose footprint no training fold touches.

```{r}
# House table format: 9 pt, centred headers, numeric right / text left,
# single line spacing.
# Supplement tables carry a hand-numbered caption, because they are labelled
# supp- rather than tbl- so that Quarto stops numbering them, and a caption
# passed here is the only one they then get.
fmt_tbl <- function(df, right = NULL, caption = NULL) {
  right_cols <- union(names(df)[vapply(df, is.numeric, TRUE)], right)
  left_cols <- setdiff(names(df), right_cols)
  ft <- flextable::flextable(df)
  ft <- flextable::fontsize(ft, size = 9, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::align(ft, align = "center", part = "header")
  if (length(right_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = right_cols, align = "right", part = "body")
  if (length(left_cols))
    ft <- flextable::align(ft, j = left_cols, align = "left", part = "body")
  ft <- flextable::line_spacing(ft, space = 1, part = "all")
  ft <- flextable::padding(ft, padding.top = 1, padding.bottom = 1,
                           part = "all")
  if (!is.null(caption)) ft <- flextable::set_caption(ft, caption)
  flextable::set_table_properties(ft, layout = "autofit", width = 1)
}
```

# Introduction

The boreal forest of Southcentral Alaska, which supplies subsistence resources, timber, wildlife habitat and carbon storage, has its dynamics governed to an unusual degree by a single biotic agent. Recurrent outbreaks of the spruce beetle, *Dendroctonus rufipennis* (Kirby, 1837), Coleoptera, Curculionidae, Scolytinae, have shaped the spruce forests of the region for centuries, with outbreak extent linked to summer temperatures [@Berg_2006]. From 1990 to 2000 an extensive outbreak caused spruce mortality across 1.19 million ha of Alaskan forest, roughly 40% more area than had been infested in the previous 70 years [@Werner_2006], and a new outbreak under way in Southcentral Alaska since about 2016 has spread from the Susitna lowlands toward the Alaska Range [@Zwieback_2024]. Identifying where and when beetle-caused mortality occurs, and at what severity, is foundational to hazard management, to carbon accounting and to understanding how a warming climate reshapes boreal disturbance regimes [@Hicke_2024], and the pressure is rising rather than steady, since a reconstruction across Europe found natural disturbance impacts increasing since 1950 [@Patacca_2022]. What that mortality costs, and what management can do about it, are set out as a research agenda by @Morris_2016, who frame outbreak impact in terms of area affected, host mortality rate and altered stand structure, the same three quantities a satellite map has to recover. Yet the operational damage record for Alaska rests on aerial sketch mapping, whose polygons carry coarse positional accuracy, record only what an observer saw from the air that year, and understate dispersed low-severity mortality [@Zwieback_2024; @Hicke_2024].

Satellite remote sensing offers the systematic record that survey flights cannot. The Landsat archive provides four decades of calibrated observation at a resolution suited to stand-scale disturbance [@Wulder_2019], and its availability in cloud platforms has made time-series analysis routine [@Gorelick_2017]. The established approach extracts temporal features from spectral index trajectories with segmentation algorithms such as LandTrendr [@Kennedy_2010] or continuous change methods such as CCDC [@Zhu_2014] and classifies them with ensemble learners, an approach mature enough to have produced an annual national record of disturbance and recovery spanning 25 years [@White_2017]. Insect damage specifically has been characterised this way, both to separate the spectral and temporal signatures of defoliators from those of bark beetles [@Meigs_2011; @Senf_2015] and to compare single-date against multi-date detection of beetle-caused mortality [@Meddens_2013]. These methods detect abrupt, stand-replacing disturbance reliably, but their outputs diverge widely for subtle change, and their skill degrades exactly where insect damage lives, on partial, gradual disturbance whose trajectories merge with natural forest variation [@Cohen_2017; @Senf_2017]. For bark beetles the mature capability is mapping the red and gray stages of heavily killed stands; low-severity and dispersed mortality remain the recognized frontier [@Senf_2017; @Hicke_2024; @Marvasti_Zadeh_2023]. That frontier is the reason aerial survey persists rather than being replaced, and reviews of the Canadian and United States survey programmes reach the same conclusion, that remote sensing can augment those methods where aerial survey consistency and spatial coverage may be insufficient for detailed monitoring across a vast forest estate [@Hall_2016; @Housman_2018].

The size of that gap in Alaska is now quantified. @Zwieback_2024 mapped dead spruce at tree scale from 2 m WorldView-2 imagery with a convolutional network at 95% average accuracy, and found that roughly 90% of beetle-killed spruce in their Southcentral study area stood in stands of areal severity below 0.05, while stand-scale Landsat shortwave infrared (SWIR) reflectance change related clearly to severity only above 0.1. In this landscape of mixed forest with low conifer fractions, nearly all mortality therefore sits beneath the detection floor of conventional Landsat change analysis. High-resolution mapping closes that gap but at the cost of proprietary imagery, which constrains both operational reuse and retrospective analysis, a trade @Hart_2015 measured directly by detecting spruce beetle mortality at both high and medium resolution. Dating the mortality rather than mapping it is a further step, and it has been attempted from daily commercial imagery [@Nowak_2026], which is the resolution this study does without. Statewide alternatives have not resolved it either, because Alaska-wide change attribution has relied on intersecting Landsat trends with the same coarse survey perimeters [@Pastick_2018], occurrence models predict beetle habitat rather than damage [@Zabihi_2021], and individual-tree mortality benchmarks, which show that spatial resolution outweighs spectral depth for detecting dead crowns, exist only outside Alaska [@Khatri_Chhetri_2024].

Deep learning applied to the temporal dimension offers a route below the index-based floor. One-dimensional convolutional networks [@Pelletier_2019] and self-attention models [@Ru_wurm_2020] classify satellite image time series without handcrafted temporal features, learning which parts of a trajectory discriminate, and the field has since accumulated recurrent detectors of disturbance [@Kong_2018], attention placed over a convolutional trunk [@Tang_2022] and self-supervised pretraining that exists because labelled time series are scarce [@Yuan_2021], surveyed by @Miller_2024. Label scarcity is the binding constraint here too, which is why the label pipeline below occupies as much of the Methods as the models do. Applied to annual Landsat subsequences over the boreal forest of eastern Canada, TempCNN and Transformer models detected and dated partial and progressive disturbances that LandTrendr-based classification missed, producing the first satellite-derived epidemic maps for the eastern spruce budworm [@Perbet_2024]. Whether that result transfers from a defoliator in Quebec to a bark beetle in Alaska is unknown, and the transfer is not trivial, since agent, host, landscape and label regime all differ, and reviews caution against porting detection results across pest-host systems [@Kautz_2024]. The European literature on *Ips typographus* (Linnaeus, 1758) is the largest body of satellite work on any bark beetle and it maps the green-attack stage from Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 [@Abdullah_2018], builds indices for early stress [@Huo_2021], tracks an outbreak crown by crown through a season [@Dalponte_2022] and separates wind damage from beetle damage in the same frame [@Candotti_2022], but its detection targets a tree that fades within one season, so its timings do not carry to a host that fades over years. The biology, however, favours Alaska. Unlike *Ips typographus*, where trees fade within months and detection races beetle emergence [@Kautz_2024], *Dendroctonus*-attacked spruce fade over years, in Alaska from green through red to gray [@Hicke_2024], so the spectral signal accumulates over time scales that annual composites resolve. What has been missing is a reference severity dataset commensurable with the satellite grid, and that now exists in the tree-scale severity product of @Zwieback_2024, released openly at 30 to 250 m stand scales, together with sub-metre statewide image mosaics on which additional reference labels can be digitised.

This study evaluates deep learning methods and an open radar time series against that reference, and tests whether feeding the models the climate variables that govern beetle development and survival, set out from the biology at the close of this Introduction, improves what they can see. It assembles a monthly Sentinel-1 radar series over Southcentral Alaska from June 2017, trains subsequence models [after @Perbet_2024] against stand-scale severity reference data, and measures them against the published SWIR detection floor [@Zwieback_2024]; the annual optical composites it built first were set aside for the measured reasons the Methods report. The objectives are to (1) quantify the skill with which an open radar time series estimates stand-scale areal severity of beetle-associated mortality, reported per severity stratum; (2) determine the detectability floor, the lowest severity stratum at which detection skill exceeds a pre-registered threshold, for each method; (3) estimate the year of mortality onset, supervised by onset intervals triangulated between the two label epochs, and quantify its lag relative to the reference record; (4) quantify the contribution of biologically motivated climate variables to detection skill; and (5) reconstruct the annual progression of the outbreak from its 2016 onset through the present across the Matanuska-Susitna Borough application extent, evaluating the reconstruction against the aerial survey archive.

Three hypotheses are tested, all over the complete outbreak trajectory from 2016 through the present rather than the single dates or two-epoch differences of prior work. Under the null (H0), temporal deep learning models do not exceed the skill of the SWIR change baseline below areal severity of 0.1, and the detection floor of @Zwieback_2024 stands. Under the alternative (H1), subsequence models achieve significantly higher detection skill than the baseline within the 0.01 to 0.10 severity stratum, lowering the floor at which freely available imagery can monitor spruce beetle mortality. The second hypothesis concerns temporal supervision, which single-date mapping cannot provide. Under H2, models trained with mortality-onset intervals triangulated between the 2020 and 2023 label epochs date onset more accurately than the same models trained on single-epoch labels. The third hypothesis carries the climate mechanism into the detection problem. Under H3, models receiving annual climate channels, a summer warmth index anchored on the 17 °C univoltinism threshold [@Hansen_2001], winter minimum temperature, and lagged summer means [@Berg_2006], detect low-severity mortality better than spectrally identical models without them. Secondarily, estimated onset years are expected to lag true onset by one to two years, as observed for gradual disturbances elsewhere in the boreal [@Perbet_2024]. The severity strata, skill metrics and decision thresholds are fixed by pre-registration before any outcome data are analysed.

The third hypothesis rests on the beetle's biology, and the climate variables it names are defined from that biology at the opening of the Methods, so the Introduction closes with the three parts of the life cycle that set them, the generation time, the manner of spread and the winter. Detection models that see only reflectance discard what those three parts imply, that a spectral decline following summers warm enough to shorten the generation is more probably beetle-caused than an identical decline that does not, although the drought evidence set out below means beetle mortality and drought stress are not fully separable by their precursors. The generation time is set in the phloem, and the season that sets it opens with flight. Adult flight in Southcentral Alaska began by the first week of June in two years of trapping, once ambient temperature rose above 12.8 °C, with most dispersal as temperatures approached and exceeded 16 °C, and attack lagged the first flights by a week or more [@Holsten_2001], so that attacks concentrate in June, in the first half of the period of rapid cambial growth of white spruce [@Hard_1985b]. Whether the brood then matures in one year or two is under direct temperature control acting on the fourth larval instar and the prepupa rather than under photoperiod, with prepupal diapause the default for larvae that have not matured by autumn [@Hansen_2001b], and the best predictor of the univoltine proportion at stand level was cumulative hours above 17 °C from 40 to 90 days after peak flight [@Hansen_2001]. The temperature that governs this is that of the phloem under direct solar radiation rather than that of the air, since two-year cycles developed on the north and west faces of standing boles at a mean phloem temperature of 10.6 °C while one-year cycles developed on the south faces of the same trees at 16.5 °C [@Werner_1985], a contrast set by aspect and canopy openness within a single stand. A warm summer therefore halves the generation time without raising fecundity, because egg production did not differ between univoltine, semivoltine and re-emerged parents, and it is the shorter generation that raises the growth rate of the population and the rate of spruce mortality in an established outbreak [@Hansen_2003]. Warming cannot add a second generation either, since an obligate adult diapause requiring a period of cold floors the life cycle at one year [@Bleiker_2019], and only a small proportion of females terminated diapause without chilling [@Davenport_2024]. Population growth between seasons is therefore stepped by the year, and the mortality a satellite series records cannot advance faster than an annual increment however warm the summer.

Spread is by threshold and by opportunity rather than along a front. The beetle relies on pheromone-mediated aggregation to raise attack density until it suffices to kill the host, and strong aggregation plumes concentrate attacks around focal trees while the anti-aggregation switching that spreads attack in the mountain pine beetle is weaker in this species [@Jenkins_2014], so mortality accumulates in foci around killed trees rather than evenly across a stand. Attack succeeds where host defence is overwhelmed and where growth is slow, since trees killed in 1982 carried a higher density of completed egg galleries than trees attacked unsuccessfully that year but did not differ from them in diameter [@Hard_1985], and diameter predicted susceptibility only where large size was coupled with slower than average radial growth over the previous five years [@Hard_1983]. Populations build in windthrown and weakened hosts before erupting onto standing stands, and windthrow and stand hazard were the two factors weighted most heavily in an expert model of outbreak risk [@Reynolds_1994], yet a blowdown alone does not start an outbreak, because major windthrow in Idaho in 1981 and 1982 preceded mortality of 350,000 trees over 90,000 ha where an extensive 1934 blowdown in Colorado produced no rise in beetle-caused mortality, so host condition, stand structure, weather and population level must all align with the fallen trees [@Jenkins_2014]. When they align the eruption is synchronous rather than radial, since the Utah population did not spread from one epicentre but erupted in many locations at once, which points to an overriding influence of temperature [@Jenkins_2014], and the Landsat record of the Southern Rocky Mountain outbreak showed the same shape, an outbreak developing at multiple incipient locations and spreading from them, synchronised by regional drivers and local dispersal together, with beetle activity strongly correlated only within about five kilometres [@Hart_2017]. Local dispersal is short, since *D. rufipennis* released in Alaska were recovered 90 to 300 m from their overwintering sites and at most 600 m away, in numbers that followed the prevailing wind [@Werner_1997]. Which regional driver synchronises the eruption is not settled as temperature alone, because in Colorado outbreaks were predicted best by interannual to multidecadal variability in drought, indexed by the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation and by summer vapour pressure deficit, and not by temperature alone [@Hart_2014], and outbreaks initiated in areas of summer, winter and multi-year drought, associated with low peak snow water equivalent and not only with summer drought [@Hart_2017]. In Alaska, the El Niño Southern Oscillation combined with late-summer drought contributed to outbreaks over one to three years while the cool phase of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation preceded them over about forty years [@Jenkins_2014], and in Interior white spruce stands cold winters usually held populations at endemic levels until those limits eased, whereupon populations increased rapidly to epidemic levels [@Holsten_1990]. The summer temperature relationship in the Alaskan record [@Berg_2006; @Sherriff_2011] therefore stands beside a moisture term rather than in place of one, and the outbreak is opportunistic in the sense that a population held at endemic level by cold or moisture erupts when the limit lifts, onto hosts already weakened.

The winter sets the last threshold, and it is a depth rather than a temperature. Larvae and adults in Alaska supercooled to about −12 °C in summer and to about −31 °C in winter, the fall carried by glycerol synthesis, and neither stage was freeze tolerant at any time of year, while temperatures measured beneath the bark of standing spruce showed that only beetles hibernating below the snow line would be expected to survive a typical winter [@Miller_1987]. Attack concentrates on the lower bole for the same reason, since that part of the stem is often below the snow line, which shields the brood from lethal cold and from woodpeckers [@Hard_1985b], and in two years of observation new attacks were first noticed and most numerous there [@Holsten_2001]. Winter minimum air temperature therefore bounds survival only for brood above the snow, and the snowpack that shelters the brood is the same one whose low peak water equivalent marked the drought-initiated outbreaks of the Southern Rockies [@Hart_2017], so a mild winter and a thin one are not the same event for this insect. Snow depth over a stand follows elevation, canopy closure and terrain, all of which the analysis grid carries, so the overwintering threshold ends as a line on the bole rather than a temperature in the air, and the measurement of the climate the models received begins from that line.

# Materials and methods

The Introduction closed on the snow line because that is where the biology stops describing the insect and starts describing the climate of a stand, and every climate variable defined for the models was defined from that biology, the warmth index from the univoltinism threshold, the winter minimum from the cold to which brood above the snow is exposed, and the lagged summer mean from the delay between a warm summer and the population it produces. The climate description was therefore placed first, before the literature, the study area and the imagery, so that the quantities the biology named are seen measured, and at what distance from the phloem temperature and the snow depth the biology turned on, before any other input is introduced. All inputs were open source, and scripted retrieval, integrity checksums and a provenance manifest accompanied the analysis code.

The sections that follow ran in the order the analysis was assembled. Climate variables defined the three channels and measured whether each varied by year or by place. Literature search recorded how the corpus was built and screened. Study area and Outbreak history placed the outbreak in its region and in the full span of the aerial survey record. Input datasets listed every source with its role and access terms, and Training data, Crown labels, Crown network and Triage queue described how reference labels were made from the two mosaic epochs. Spectral separability, Survey polygons and Radar record built the predictor record, and Satellite composites, Composite assembly and Analysis cube record the optical record that was built first and set aside, with the measurements that set it aside. Subsequence sampling, Architectures, Baseline model and Model training defined what was fitted, Endmember calibration and Pipeline validation tested the pipeline on synthetic stands before any label was scored, and Model evaluation set out the cross-validation and the tests of the three hypotheses.

## Climate variables

The biology named phloem temperature and snow depth, and neither was observed at stand scale across the outbreak years, so the channels were built from the gridded daily air temperature record standing nearest to both. Daily minimum and maximum air temperature from the Daymet version 4 gridded forcings at 1 km resolution [@Thornton_2021] were reduced, per 90 m stand cell and year, to three biologically motivated variables, namely a summer warmth index, the cumulative degree-hours above 17 °C from June through September, a fixed-window approximation of the univoltinism predictor of @Hansen_2001, whose original formulation counts hours above that threshold from 40 to 90 days after peak flight; the winter minimum daily temperature from November through March, indexing the cold to which brood above the snow line was exposed, the snow depth that governed survival below it lying outside the pre-registered channels; and the two-year lagged mean summer temperature, following the lagged temperature association in the regional outbreak record [@Berg_2006; @Sherriff_2011]. @fig-climate shows the three variables over the study window from 1990 through the most recent complete Daymet year, with the seasonal integration windows drawn from the biology, June through September for the warmth index, when development above the 17 °C threshold accrues [@Hansen_2001], and November through March for the winter minimum, when the overwintering stages are exposed [@Werner_2006; @Bentz_2010]. The regional series was computed live from the daily forcings and cached.

```{r}
#| label: climate-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
clim_f <- file.path(inputs, "derived", "climate_series.csv")
if (!file.exists(clim_f)) {
  library(rgee)
  ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  tpl_c <- rast(file.path(inputs, "zwieback-severity", "merged_ref_h_c90c.tif"))
  bbc <- as.vector(ext(project(as.polygons(ext(tpl_c) + 50000,
                                           crs = crs(tpl_c)), "EPSG:4326")))
  roi_c <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(bbc[1], bbc[3], bbc[2], bbc[4]))
  dm <- ee$ImageCollection("NASA/ORNL/DAYMET_V4")
  yearly <- function(y) {
    smr <- dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-06-01", y), sprintf("%d-10-01", y))
    tmean <- smr$map(function(img)
      img$select("tmax")$add(img$select("tmin"))$divide(2)$rename("tmean"))
    gdd <- tmean$map(function(img)
      img$subtract(17)$max(0)$multiply(24))$sum()$rename("warmth")
    smean <- tmean$mean()$rename("summer_mean")
    wtr <- dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-11-01", y - 1), sprintf("%d-04-01", y))$
      select("tmin")$min()$rename("winter_min")
    gdd$addBands(smean)$addBands(wtr)$reduceRegion(
      reducer = ee$Reducer$mean(), geometry = roi_c, scale = 1000,
      maxPixels = 1e10)
  }
  years <- 1990:2023
  vals <- lapply(years, function(y) unlist(yearly(y)$getInfo()))
  clim <- data.frame(year = years, do.call(rbind, vals))
  clim$summer_mean_lag2 <- c(NA, NA, head(clim$summer_mean, -2))
  dir.create(dirname(clim_f), showWarnings = FALSE)
  write.csv(clim, clim_f, row.names = FALSE)
}
clim <- read.csv(clim_f)
```

Per-cell channel rasters were exported at Daymet's native 1 km resolution for each year, for resampling to the stand grid when subsequences are assembled.

```{r}
#| label: climate-rasters
#| echo: true
#| output: false
clim_dir <- file.path(inputs, "climate")
dir.create(clim_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
todo_c <- (2012:2023)[!file.exists(file.path(clim_dir,
                                             sprintf("clim_%d.tif", 2012:2023)))]
if (length(todo_c)) {
  library(rgee)
  ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  tpl_c <- rast(file.path(inputs, "zwieback-severity", "merged_ref_h_c90c.tif"))
  bbc <- as.vector(ext(project(as.polygons(ext(tpl_c) + 50000,
                                           crs = crs(tpl_c)), "EPSG:4326")))
  roi_c <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(bbc[1], bbc[3], bbc[2], bbc[4]))
  dm <- ee$ImageCollection("NASA/ORNL/DAYMET_V4")
  for (y in todo_c) {
    smr <- dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-06-01", y), sprintf("%d-10-01", y))
    tmean <- smr$map(function(img)
      img$select("tmax")$add(img$select("tmin"))$divide(2)$rename("tmean"))
    img <- tmean$map(function(im) im$subtract(17)$max(0)$multiply(24))$sum()$
      rename("warmth")$
      addBands(tmean$mean()$rename("summer_mean"))$
      addBands(dm$filterDate(sprintf("%d-11-01", y - 1),
                             sprintf("%d-04-01", y))$
                 select("tmin")$min()$rename("winter_min"))
    url <- img$toFloat()$getDownloadURL(list(region = roi_c,
                                             scale = 1000,
                                             crs = "EPSG:32605",
                                             format = "GEO_TIFF"))
    f <- file.path(clim_dir, sprintf("clim_%d.tif", y))
    old_to <- options(timeout = 600)
    try(download.file(url, f, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
    options(old_to)
  }
}
```

@fig-climograph gives the seasonal setting the annual variables above are integrated from, so that the June to September window and the 17 °C threshold can be read against the temperature regime they sit in rather than taken on assertion, and it is reduced from the same daily Daymet forcings from which climate values are to be fitted at the radar's monthly step.

```{r}
#| label: climograph-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Monthly climatology from the same Daymet version 4 forcings the annual
# variables are built from, reduced server-side one calendar month at a time so
# the whole daily archive never has to be pulled. Written once and read
# thereafter, on the pattern every other input chunk here follows.
mon_f <- file.path(inputs, "derived", "climate_monthly.csv")
if (!file.exists(mon_f)) {
  library(rgee)
  ee_Initialize(project = "murphys-deforisk", quiet = TRUE)
  # The extent comes from a climate raster already built for this study rather
  # than from the severity reference. A climograph needs a bounding box, not a
  # severity value, and reading the reference here would put a sixth chunk on
  # the list of those that touch it before the analysis is unblocked.
  tpl_m <- rast(file.path(inputs, "climate", "clim_2016.tif"))
  bbm <- as.vector(ext(project(as.polygons(ext(tpl_m), crs = crs(tpl_m)),
                               "EPSG:4326")))
  aoi_m <- ee$Geometry$Rectangle(c(bbm[1], bbm[3], bbm[2], bbm[4]))
  dm <- ee$ImageCollection("NASA/ORNL/DAYMET_V4")$
    filterDate("1990-01-01", "2024-01-01")$filterBounds(aoi_m)
  rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:12, function(m) {
    sub <- dm$filter(ee$Filter$calendarRange(m, m, "month"))
    img <- sub$select(c("tmax", "tmin"))$mean()$
      addBands(sub$select("prcp")$mean()$multiply(
        c(31,28,31,30,31,30,31,31,30,31,30,31)[m])$rename("prcp_month"))
    v <- img$reduceRegion(reducer = ee$Reducer$mean(), geometry = aoi_m,
                          scale = 1000, maxPixels = 1e9, bestEffort = TRUE)$
      getInfo()
    data.frame(month = m, tmax = v$tmax, tmin = v$tmin, prcp = v$prcp_month)
  }))
  rows$tmean <- (rows$tmax + rows$tmin) / 2
  write.csv(rows, mon_f, row.names = FALSE)
}
clim_m <- read.csv(mon_f)
clim_m$month_name <- month.abb[clim_m$month]
```

```{r}
#| label: climograph-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
warm_m <- clim_m[which.max(clim_m$tmax), ]
```

The threshold sits above the season rather than inside it. The warmest month was `r month.name[warm_m$month]`, whose mean daily maximum over 1990 to 2023 was `r sprintf("%.1f", warm_m$tmax)` °C, so on an average day of the warmest month the temperature did not reach the 17 °C univoltinism threshold at all and degree-hours accrue only on the warmer days within the window. That is why the warmth index varies so strongly between years, and it is the reason a summer that runs a degree above normal changes the generation time of a population that an average summer leaves on a two-year cycle [@Hansen_2001].

```{r}
#| label: fig-climograph
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Climograph of the study area from Daymet version 4 daily forcings averaged over 1990 to 2023, monthly mean precipitation as bars against monthly mean, maximum and minimum daily air temperature. The horizontal line marks the 17 °C threshold above which spruce beetle development accrues toward a one-year generation, and the shaded band marks June through September, the window over which the summer warmth index integrates. Adult flight occurs in early summer, at the opening of that band."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.2
# Precipitation is drawn from a baseline at the floor of the temperature axis
# rather than from zero. Sharing zero puts the bars over the winter curves and
# makes the right-hand axis run negative, which is a precipitation no station
# has ever recorded.
base <- floor(min(clim_m$tmin) / 5) * 5
sc <- max(clim_m$prcp) / (max(clim_m$tmax) - base)
# The month axis is numeric so the bars can be drawn as rectangles standing on
# the baseline. geom_col always starts a bar at zero, which here would hang the
# drier months below the axis.
ggplot(clim_m, aes(x = month)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 5.5, xmax = 9.5, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey85", alpha = .55) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = month - .35, xmax = month + .35, ymin = base,
                ymax = base + prcp / sc), fill = "steelblue4", alpha = .75) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 17, linetype = "22", colour = "#C0392B") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.4, y = 18.2, label = "17 °C univoltinism threshold",
           size = 2.5, colour = "#C0392B", hjust = 0) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmax, colour = "Daily maximum"), linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmean, colour = "Daily mean"), linewidth = .6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = tmin, colour = "Daily minimum"), linewidth = .5) +
  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("Daily maximum" = "#E67E22",
                                       "Daily mean" = "grey20",
                                       "Daily minimum" = "steelblue4")) +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Temperature (°C)",
                     sec.axis = sec_axis(~ (. - base) * sc,
                                         name = "Precipitation (mm)")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, expand = c(.01, .01)) +
  labs(x = NULL) + th + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-climate
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Annual climate variables over the study window from Daymet version 4 daily forcings, 1990 to 2023. (a) Summer warmth index, the cumulative degree-hours above 17 °C from June to September, the seasonal window in which development above the univoltinism threshold accrues. (b) Winter minimum daily temperature, November to March, when overwintering stages beneath the bark are exposed to cold mortality; the two-year lagged summer mean tracks the delayed population response. The dashed line marks the 2016 outbreak onset."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
library(patchwork)
pa <- ggplot(clim, aes(year, warmth)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#C0392B", width = .75) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2016, linetype = "22", colour = "grey30") +
  labs(title = "(a) Summer warmth index", y = "Degree-hours > 17 °C",
       x = NULL) + th
pb <- ggplot(clim, aes(year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = winter_min, colour = "Winter minimum"), linewidth = .5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = summer_mean_lag2, colour = "Summer mean, lag 2 yr"),
            linewidth = .5) +

  scale_colour_manual(NULL, values = c("Winter minimum" = "steelblue4",
                                       "Summer mean, lag 2 yr" = "#E67E22")) +
  labs(title = "(b) Winter minimum and lagged summer mean",
       y = "°C", x = NULL) + th + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

```

The three annual channels were defined and computed as above, and they are what the third hypothesis names in the pre-registration. The design of 2026-09-09 fits temporally corresponding climate values to the model at the radar's monthly step, before classification, from the same daily Daymet forcings the climograph is reduced from; that fit is the design and has not been built, so what stands is the annual channels and the monthly record they will be fitted from. Daymet extended through 2023 when the analysis was run, and later years carry an availability flag in place of measured values until the forcing series updates.

```{r}
#| label: climate-variance
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Whether these channels carry timing information, spatial information or both,
# measured over the blocks the models actually see rather than over the whole
# frame, which includes the Alaska Range and inflates the spatial spread.
climvar_f <- file.path(root, "03.outputs", "climate_variance.csv")
if (!file.exists(climvar_f)) {
  cf <- sort(list.files(file.path(inputs, "climate"),
                        pattern = "^clim_[0-9]{4}[.]tif$", full.names = TRUE))
  blk_c <- sf::st_read(file.path(inputs, "derived", "sample_blocks.gpkg"),
                       quiet = TRUE)
  nm <- c("summer warmth index", "winter minimum", "lagged summer mean")
  cv <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:3, function(b) {
    st <- rast(lapply(cf, function(x) rast(x)[[b]]))
    v <- terra::extract(st, vect(sf::st_transform(blk_c, crs(st))),
                        fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
    v <- v[stats::complete.cases(v), ]
    data.frame(channel = nm[b], blocks = nrow(v),
               between_year = sd(colMeans(v)),
               between_block = mean(apply(v, 2, sd)))
  }))
  cv$ratio <- cv$between_year / cv$between_block
  write.csv(cv, climvar_f, row.names = FALSE)
}
climvar <- read.csv(climvar_f)
cvr <- function(ch) climvar$ratio[climvar$channel == ch]
```

Whether these channels carry timing or place was measured rather than asserted, over the `r climvar$blocks[1]` sampled blocks of the cross-validation design described below rather than the whole frame, whose mountains would inflate any spatial spread. The three do not behave alike. The summer warmth index varies `r sprintf("%.2f", cvr("summer warmth index"))` times as much between years as between blocks, so it is chiefly a timing channel. The winter minimum and the two-year lagged summer mean do the opposite, at `r sprintf("%.2f", cvr("winter minimum"))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", cvr("lagged summer mean"))`, varying more between blocks within a year than between years. Two of the three therefore carry spatial contrast the network can use to tell one stand from another, which is more than a timing channel can offer and more than the design assumed. The third hypothesis is correspondingly better posed than it would be if all three were regional series broadcast to every cell, because a channel with no spatial variation could only shift a prediction year by year, never stand by stand. @fig-warmth-map shows the summer warmth index over the blocks in the warmest and the coolest year of the raster record, which is what a timing channel looks like on the ground.

```{r}
#| label: warmth-map-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
clim_raster_years <- subset(clim, year %in% 2012:2023)
warm_cool <- clim_raster_years$year[c(which.max(clim_raster_years$warmth),
                                      which.min(clim_raster_years$warmth))]
warmth <- rast(sprintf("../02.inputs/climate/clim_%d.tif", warm_cool),
               lyrs = c(1, 4)) |>
  crop(st_buffer(st_as_sfc(st_bbox(blocks)), 5000))
names(warmth) <- warm_cool
warmth_lim <- range(values(warmth), na.rm = TRUE)
warmth_map_cap <- paste0(
  "Summer warmth index, the cumulative degree-hours above 17 °C from June to ",
  "September, from the Daymet version 4 rasters at ", res(warmth)[1] / 1000,
  " km over the sampled blocks, in (a) ", warm_cool[1], ", the warmest year of ",
  "the raster record, and (b) ", warm_cool[2], ", the coolest, on one colour ",
  "range from ", round(warmth_lim[1]), " to ", format(round(warmth_lim[2]), big.mark = ","),
  " degree-hours. The regional mean was ",
  format(round(clim$warmth[clim$year == warm_cool[1]]), big.mark = ","),
  " degree-hours in the warm year and ",
  round(clim$warmth[clim$year == warm_cool[2]]), " in the cool one, so the cool ",
  "year is nearly blank on a scale that the warm year fills, which is the ",
  "sense in which the channel carries timing rather than place. Grey points ",
  "are the ", nrow(blocks), " sampled blocks. WGS 84 UTM zone 5N (EPSG:32605), ",
  "graticule in km."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-warmth-map
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: !expr warmth_map_cap
#| fig-width: 7

warmth_panel <- function(lyr, title, legend) {
  tm_shape(in_km(warmth[[lyr]])) +
    tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_continuous(values = "-brewer.yl_or_rd",

}

  warmth_panel(1, sprintf("(a) %d, warmest year", warm_cool[1]), tm_legend_hide()),
  warmth_panel(2, sprintf("(b) %d, coolest year", warm_cool[2]),
               tm_legend(title = "Degree-hours", reverse = TRUE, height = 8,
```

## Literature search

The corpus this study is argued against was assembled by a search run on 2026-09-08 over OpenAlex and arXiv, with every retained record verified against Crossref by content negotiation on its digital object identifier before it entered the bibliography. Six strands were searched. Five took their keywords from the title, namely spruce beetle with remote sensing, deep learning over satellite image time series, low-severity and partial disturbance detection, bark beetle mortality mapping, and boreal Alaskan forest disturbance, each restricted to 2010 and later. The sixth, on harmonisation between the Operational Land Imager and the MultiSpectral Instrument, was added on 2026-09-08 after the trajectory of the analysis cube showed a reflectance step at the sensor boundary, so that strand answers a question the data raised rather than one the title anticipated. Records were retained where they reported a method for detecting or mapping insect-caused tree mortality from satellite or airborne imagery, supplied a deep learning architecture for satellite image time series, or reported spruce beetle outbreak ecology bearing on the climate mechanism tested here; records reporting agriculture, fire, land cover, tundra or carbon cycle work were excluded, as were sensor descriptions carrying no detection method.

```{r}
#| label: lit-screening
#| echo: true
#| output: false
scr <- read.csv(file.path(inputs, "derived", "literature_screening.csv"))
n_screened <- nrow(scr)
n_included <- sum(scr$decision == "included")
n_strands <- length(unique(scr$strand))
```

The search returned `r n_screened` unique records across `r n_strands` strands after duplicates were removed, of which `r n_included` were retained and `r n_screened - n_included` excluded. The screening table is committed with the manuscript at `02.inputs/derived/literature_screening.csv`, one row per record with its strand, its decision and the reason for that decision, so the counts above are read at render time rather than written down.

## Study area

The study area is the Southcentral Alaska outbreak region, centred on the Susitna lowlands and Matanuska-Susitna Valley and bounded by the Talkeetna Mountains and the Alaska Range, in the NAD83 Alaska Albers projection. Forests are boreal mosaics of white spruce (*Picea glauca* (Moench) Voss), black spruce (*P. mariana* (Mill.) Britton et al.), Alaska birch (*Betula neoalaskana* Sarg.) and trembling aspen (*Populus tremuloides* Michx.), with wetlands and mixed stands in which conifer fractions of 10 to 30% predominate [@Zwieback_2024]. The ongoing outbreak reached the area around 2016 and had exhausted much of the large white spruce by 2021 [@Zwieback_2024]. The nearest precedent for what follows such an outbreak is the Kenai Peninsula, where the 1987 to 2000 event was tracked through its vegetation change and forest regeneration [@Boucher_2006] and where stand susceptibility in Lutz and Sitka spruce had already been classified from stand structure [@Roynolds_1996]. The temporal window of the study spans the full history of this outbreak, from its onset around 2016 through the most recent survey year, observed by annual Sentinel-2 and Landsat composites; earlier Landsat years enter only as the undisturbed pre-outbreak baseline against which the outbreak trajectory was measured. Model training and cross-validation blocks span the confirmatory study window, a 39,050 km2 frame around the reference footprint; the Talkeetna to Byers Lake footprint of the independent severity reference serves as the held-out evaluation area for the severity product. A larger application extent, the Matanuska-Susitna Borough, receives the trained model's wall-to-wall severity and progression maps for management use; predictions outside the confirmatory window are application products whose transfer was not confirmed by the cross-validation, and were labelled accordingly. One limit follows from that choice of extent and is stated here rather than deferred. The design samples one outbreak in one region, so nothing in it estimates how the models would transfer to the Kenai Peninsula, to Interior Alaska or to another *Dendroctonus* system, and the cross-validation bounds error within this region alone. Severity summaries are additionally reported per stand of the state Mat-Su Borough forest inventory for use by forest managers.

All spatial figures shared one cartographic standard. The working grid was WGS 84 UTM zone 5N, matching the severity reference grid, graticules were drawn in the same projected grid in kilometres, and every map carried its coordinate reference system, a scale bar and a north arrow. @fig-studyarea locates the sampled blocks and their folds over the terrain, with the recorded outbreak footprint and the boundary between UTM zones 5 and 6, which crosses the study window.

## Outbreak history

The aerial detection survey has recorded spruce beetle damage in Alaska since 1997, and reading its whole span rather than the years this study models puts the present outbreak in its place. @fig-spread draws it.

```{r}
#| label: spread-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The full survey record rather than the study window. Centroids are taken in
# the archive's own projected system and only then transformed to geographic
# coordinates, because several polygons carry duplicate vertices that the
# spherical geometry engine rejects.
spread_f <- file.path(root, "03.outputs", "survey_spread.csv")
if (!file.exists(spread_f)) {
  sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
  q <- paste("SELECT SURVEY_YEAR, ACRES, Shape FROM",
             "DAMAGE_AREAS_FLAT_AllYears_AK_Rgn10",
             "WHERE DCA_COMMON_NAME LIKE '%spruce beetle%'")
  pg <- sf::st_read(file.path(inputs, "ids-region10",
                              "AK_Region10_AllYears.gdb"),
                    query = q, quiet = TRUE)
  ll <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(
    suppressWarnings(sf::st_centroid(sf::st_geometry(pg))), 4326))
  sp <- data.frame(year = pg$SURVEY_YEAR, acres = pg$ACRES,
                   lat = ll[, 2], lon = ll[, 1])
  sp <- sp[stats::complete.cases(sp) & sp$acres > 0, ]
  sp$hectares <- sp$acres * 0.40468564
  write.csv(sp, spread_f, row.names = FALSE)
}
spread <- read.csv(spread_f)
spread_yr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(spread, spread$year), function(d)
  data.frame(year = d$year[1],
             lat = sum(d$lat * d$hectares) / sum(d$hectares),
             kha = sum(d$hectares) / 1000)))
spread_fit <- lm(lat ~ year, spread_yr)
```

Across `r nrow(spread_yr)` survey years the area-weighted mean latitude of recorded damage moved north by `r sprintf("%.2f", coef(spread_fit)[2] * diff(range(spread_yr$year)))` degrees, about `r sprintf("%.0f", coef(spread_fit)[2] * diff(range(spread_yr$year)) * 111)` km \[F(1, `r spread_fit$df.residual`) = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(spread_fit)$fstatistic[1])`, p = `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(spread_fit)$coefficients[2, 4])`, R² = `r sprintf("%.3f", summary(spread_fit)$r.squared)`\]. Three things bound that number. The trend explains under a quarter of the year-to-year variance, so it describes a drift rather than a march. The survey records where observers flew, so a shift in the recorded centre is partly a shift in effort. And the mass at the start of the record is the Kenai Peninsula outbreak while the mass at the end is the Susitna lowlands, so this is the centre of recorded damage moving between two events rather than one population tracked as it moves.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spread
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Spruce beetle damage recorded by the Alaska aerial detection survey, 1997 to 2025, from all 33,015 polygons the survey attributes to the agent. (a) Damage area by quarter-degree latitude band and survey year, on a square-root colour scale so the smaller years remain visible. (b) The area-weighted mean latitude of damage in each year, sized by the area recorded that year, with a least-squares line and its interval. The survey records where observers flew, so the recorded centre reflects survey effort as well as beetle activity."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.4
spread$band <- floor(spread$lat * 4) / 4
sp_grid <- aggregate(hectares ~ band + year, spread, sum)
ps_a <- ggplot(sp_grid, aes(year, band, fill = hectares / 1000)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt",
                       name = "kha") +
  labs(title = "(a) Recorded damage by latitude", x = NULL,
       y = "Latitude (degrees north)") + th
ps_b <- ggplot(spread_yr, aes(year, lat)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "#C0392B", fill = "#C0392B",
              alpha = .15, linewidth = .5, formula = y ~ x) +
  geom_point(aes(size = kha), colour = "steelblue4", alpha = .85) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(.8, 4.5), name = "kha") +
  labs(title = "(b) Area-weighted mean latitude", x = NULL,
       y = "Latitude (degrees north)") + th
ps_a / ps_b
```

## Input datasets

The study draws on nine input datasets in four roles (@tbl-inputs). Reference data were what the models learned from and were judged against, namely the crown delineations digitised for this study on the two State of Alaska Maxar mosaic epochs, seeded by the released labels and network of @Zwieback_2024, and the independent severity rasters of the same study. Predictor data were what the models saw, the annual Sentinel-2 and Landsat composites. Terrain and conifer fraction [@Macander_2022] conditioned sampling and interpretation. The aerial detection survey polygons and their flown-area footprints gave weak spatial context, stratifying the sample and separating surveyed absence from non-survey. The downloadable reference and context datasets are checksum-verified at retrieval; predictor assembly precedes no outcome analysis, which waits behind pre-registration.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-inputs

                 "polygon", "10-20 m", "30 m", "5 m", "30 m"),
```

## Training data

Stand-scale areal severity of beetle-associated dead spruce for the Talkeetna to Byers Lake area in 2021, derived by @Zwieback_2024 from a convolutional network applied to WorldView-2 imagery, and therefore a model product with its own documented error structure rather than ground truth, so agreement with it bounds map accuracy rather than establishing it, was used at three released stand scales solely for independent evaluation. Metadata were inspected here; values are neither summarised nor plotted before pre-registration.

```{r}
#| label: severity-metadata
#| echo: true
sev <- lapply(c("merged_ref_h_c30c.tif", "merged_ref_h_c90c.tif",
                "merged_ref_h_c250c.tif"),
              function(f) rast(file.path(inputs, "zwieback-severity", f)))
data.frame(
  file       = vapply(sev, function(r) basename(sources(r)), ""),
  resolution = vapply(sev, function(r) paste(round(res(r)), collapse = " x "), ""),
  ncell      = vapply(sev, ncell, numeric(1)),
  crs        = vapply(sev, function(r) st_crs(crs(r))$Name, "")
)
```

## Crown labels

Reference labels were produced by machine-assisted digitisation of dead spruce crowns on the statewide sub-metre mosaics, acquired in 2020 at 0.5 m and in 2023 at 0.3 m resolution, over sample blocks stratified by conifer fraction and survey-recorded damage history. Imagery was obtained as four-band chips from the USDA NRCS image services, whose export endpoint carries the same mosaics. The route is public but the pixels are not, since the service records the Alaska Vivid imagery as a dataset licensed from Maxar to USDA-FPAC in 2020, with copyright retained by the vendor. Imagery was therefore processed locally and never redistributed, and what this study publishes from it are the derived crown delineations and stand-level severity fractions, not the pixels, on the same footing as the published delineations of @Zwieback_2024, which were drawn on proprietary imagery that their release could not include. Label preparation runs in four stages.

1.  **Pre-labelling.** The released dead-spruce network of @Zwieback_2024 is the only domain-tuned component available, but it cannot be applied to these mosaics as released. It was trained on seven pansharpened WorldView-2 bands, blue, green, yellow, red, red edge and two near-infrared bands, and its encoder's first layer was widened from three channels to seven to match; the four-band mosaics used here supply no yellow, red-edge or second near-infrared channel. The network was therefore adapted rather than applied. The first-layer weights for the four channels the two sensors share were retained, the remaining three discarded, and the network fine-tuned on the published crown labels of the same study, which were rasterised against mosaic imagery over their own delineation areas. Those areas, not the sample blocks, supply the tuning imagery, because the delineations intersect only four blocks and all four fall in the held-out reference fold.
2.  **Crown segmentation.** Candidate detections were refined into crown polygons with general-purpose segmentation models, DeepForest crown detection [@Weinstein_2019] supplying box prompts to the Segment Anything Model (SAM2) through the segment-geospatial toolchain [@Wu_2023], an established zero-shot pipeline for tree delineation. Segmentation runs on the project's cloud GPU; outputs are vector crown candidates scored by the dead-spruce probability.
3.  **Cleaning and triage.** Candidates below a minimum crown area or outside plausible crown geometry were dropped; overlapping detections were merged. Two annotators then accept, edit or reject each candidate independently in QGIS, with a third adjudicating disagreements [after @Khatri_Chhetri_2024]. Fully occluded dead spruce under closed deciduous canopy remain undetectable in RGB imagery and are an acknowledged limitation carried forward from @Zwieback_2024.
4.  **Aggregation, triangulation and classification.** Accepted crowns were rasterised to stand-cell areal severity fractions at 30 and 90 m, Mortality agent was inferred from context throughout, since no crown was confirmed by ground observation, so other agents of spruce death enter the labels as beetle kill at a rate this design cannot measure. Crown polygons were rasterised to stand-cell areal severity fractions at 30 and 90 m, and each labelled stand was classified as low, medium or high disturbance at the pre-registered severity breaks. Cross-epoch triangulation then assigned every crown a temporal state, either dead by 2020, died between 2020 and 2023, or alive through 2023, yielding interval-censored onset labels for the dating head, verified pre-mortality trajectories for exploratory green-stage analysis, and confirmed-alive negatives. The same comparison cleaned the labels, since a crown dead in 2020 must remain dead in 2023, and violations were returned to triage, a consistency check unavailable to single-epoch designs.

The published crown labels of @Zwieback_2024, distributed under an attribution licence, additionally enter the training pool within their delineation areas, contributing temporal cuts at their image dates of 2018 and 2021. Combined with the 2020 and 2023 mosaic epochs, four temporal cuts are available in the Talkeetna to Byers Lake area, narrowing onset brackets there to one to two years. The severity rasters of @Zwieback_2024, by contrast, take no part in label preparation; they remain the untouched independent evaluation dataset described under Model evaluation.

Tuning pairs were assembled below. For each delineation area holding crowns, a four-band chip at the 2020 mosaic resolution and the matching crown mask rasterised from the published polygons. The crowns were delineated on imagery of August 2021, one year after the 2020 mosaic, so a crown that died during that year was marked dead over imagery in which it was still living. This is label noise of known sign, and it is one-directional, in that it can only teach the network that living crowns are dead, never the reverse. Its size was bounded by the fraction of crowns dying in that single year and was reported with the pairs.

```{r}
#| label: label-training-pairs
#| echo: true
#| output: false
lab_dir <- file.path(inputs, "zwieback-labels", "gpkg")
pair_dir <- file.path(inputs, "label-pairs")
dir.create(pair_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
lab_f <- list.files(lab_dir, pattern = "_labels[.]gpkg$", full.names = TRUE)
pairs_csv <- file.path(dirname(inputs), "03.outputs", "label_pairs.csv")

if (!file.exists(pairs_csv)) {
  library(sf)
  GSD <- 0.5                       # 2020 mosaic ground sample distance, metres
  rows <- list()
  options(timeout = 300)
  for (f in lab_f) {
    l <- suppressWarnings(st_read(f, quiet = TRUE))
    if (nrow(l) == 0) next
    id <- sub("_labels[.]gpkg$", "", basename(f))
    # One delivered file (area 0033, 73 crowns) declares EPSG:4326 while its
    # coordinates are UTM zone 5N metres, which makes st_area report a crown as
    # billions of square metres. Relabel without transforming; the coordinates
    # were always UTM.
    if (!identical(st_crs(l)$epsg, 32605L)) {
      bb0 <- suppressWarnings(st_bbox(l))
      if (bb0[["xmin"]] > 1000) l <- st_set_crs(l, 32605)
    }
    bb <- st_bbox(l)
    px <- round(c(bb["xmax"] - bb["xmin"], bb["ymax"] - bb["ymin"]) / GSD)
    img_f <- file.path(pair_dir, sprintf("%s_img.tif", id))
    msk_f <- file.path(pair_dir, sprintf("%s_mask.tif", id))
    if (!file.exists(img_f)) {
      u <- sprintf(paste0(
        "https://apps.geo.fpac.usda.gov/nrcs-imagery/rest/services/",
        "ortho_imagery/alaska_vivid_2020_50cm/ImageServer/exportImage?",
        "bbox=%f,%f,%f,%f&bboxSR=32605&imageSR=32605&size=%d,%d",
        "&format=tiff&f=image"),
        bb["xmin"], bb["ymin"], bb["xmax"], bb["ymax"], px[1], px[2])
      ok <- FALSE
      for (attempt in 1:3) {          # the public service drops requests
        ok <- !inherits(try(download.file(u, img_f, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE),
                            silent = TRUE), "try-error")
        if (ok && inherits(try(rast(img_f), silent = TRUE), "try-error")) {
          unlink(img_f); ok <- FALSE  # HTML error body, not imagery
        }
        if (ok) break
        Sys.sleep(2)
      }
      # A silent `next` here would drop the area from the table and make a
      # failed fetch look like an area that never had crowns.
      if (!ok) {
        rows[[id]] <- data.frame(area = id, crowns = nrow(l),
          chip_px = "FETCH FAILED", bands = NA_integer_,
          crown_area_m2 = round(sum(as.numeric(st_area(l)))),
          pct_crown = NA_real_)
        next
      }
      Sys.sleep(0.5)
    }
    img <- rast(img_f)
    if (!file.exists(msk_f)) {
      m <- rasterize(vect(l), rast(img[[1]]), field = 1, background = 0)
      writeRaster(m, msk_f, overwrite = TRUE, datatype = "INT1U")
    }
    m <- rast(msk_f)
    rows[[id]] <- data.frame(
      area = id, crowns = nrow(l),
      chip_px = sprintf("%d x %d", ncol(img), nrow(img)),
      bands = nlyr(img),
      crown_area_m2 = round(sum(as.numeric(st_area(l)))),
      pct_crown = round(100 * global(m, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1], 2))
  }
  write.csv(do.call(rbind, rows), pairs_csv, row.names = FALSE)
}
pairs <- read.csv(pairs_csv)
```

The tuning pairs are listed in Table S1. Of `r nrow(pairs)` delineation areas holding crowns, `r sum(!is.na(pairs$bands))` yielded imagery, carrying `r format(sum(pairs$crowns[!is.na(pairs$bands)]), big.mark = ",")` of the `r format(sum(pairs$crowns), big.mark = ",")` published crowns over `r format(sum(pairs$crown_area_m2[!is.na(pairs$bands)]), big.mark = ",")` m² of delineated dead canopy; dead crowns occupy `r sprintf("%.1f%%", mean(pairs$pct_crown, na.rm = TRUE))` of chip pixels on average. That imbalance is the reason the parent study weighted the dead class twenty times the background class, and the same weighting carries over here. Two properties of the delivered labels are worth recording, since neither was documented with them. One area declared a geographic coordinate reference system while holding projected coordinates, which inflates its computed crown areas by nine orders of magnitude if taken at face value, and the delineation areas vary in size by more than two orders of magnitude, so the smallest carry too few pixels to serve as training chips and were dropped at the tiling stage rather than here.

## Crown network

The released network was adapted to the four bands these mosaics carry and fine-tuned on the tuning pairs above. Its first convolution was widened by @Zwieback_2024 from three channels to seven to match pansharpened WorldView-2, in the band order blue, green, yellow, red, red edge, near infrared-1 and near infrared-2. The mosaics here are blue, green, red and near infrared, an ordering confirmed from the imagery rather than assumed. The fourth band reached a 95th percentile far above the visible bands with a floor near zero over water and shadow, which is near-infrared behaviour, and among the visible bands the third was least correlated with it, which is red under chlorophyll absorption. The four matching input filters were therefore copied from the released weights and the three with no counterpart discarded, so tuning starts from learned dead-spruce features rather than from noise. Dead crowns occupy a small minority of pixels, so the loss weights that class twenty to one following the parent study. Areas are split by area, never by tile, so no crop of a validation area is ever seen in training.

The chunk below runs as its own process rather than through reticulate. The manuscript has already loaded sits, which loads the R binding to libtorch, and initialising Python's torch in the same process loads a second copy of that library and segfaults the session. Running the interpreter as a subprocess keeps the two apart, and the interpreter was named explicitly because the environment's default resolves to a build that carries no torch.

```{python}
#| label: crown-finetune
#| echo: true
#| output: false
#| python.reticulate: false
#| engine.path: /opt/local/bin/python3
import os, glob, csv, numpy as np, rasterio, torch, torch.nn as nn

root = os.path.abspath(os.path.join("..", ""))
pair_dir = os.path.join(root, "02.inputs", "label-pairs")
ckpt = os.path.join(root, "02.inputs", "crown_net_4band.pt")
metrics_csv = os.path.join(root, "03.outputs", "crown_net_metrics.csv")

TILE, STRIDE, EPOCHS, DEAD_W = 512, 384, 8, 20.0
# Our band order (blue, green, red, NIR) mapped onto the released model's
# seven WorldView-2 channels (blue, green, yellow, red, red edge, NIR1, NIR2).
KEEP = [0, 1, 3, 5]

# Tiles are indexed, not materialised. Holding all crops in memory costs about
# 580 MB on top of an R session that already holds the composites, which on this
# 8 GB machine drives the process into swap and stalls it; a windowed read per
# crop keeps the footprint to the batch in hand.
def index_of(area):
    with rasterio.open(os.path.join(pair_dir, area + "_img.tif")) as s:
        h, w = s.height, s.width
    # Areas smaller than a tile are padded rather than discarded. Dropping them
    # cost 8 of 37 areas and about a fifth of the delineated crowns, which at
    # this sample size matters more than the edge artefact padding introduces.
    if h < TILE or w < TILE:
        return [(area, 0, 0)]
    return [(area, y, x)
            for y in range(0, h - TILE + 1, STRIDE)
            for x in range(0, w - TILE + 1, STRIDE)]

def load(item, augment=False):
    area, y, x = item
    win = rasterio.windows.Window(x, y, TILE, TILE)
    with rasterio.open(os.path.join(pair_dir, area + "_img.tif")) as s:
        img = s.read(window=win).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    with rasterio.open(os.path.join(pair_dir, area + "_mask.tif")) as s:
        msk = s.read(1, window=win).astype(np.int64)
    if img.shape[1] < TILE or img.shape[2] < TILE:
        py, px = TILE - img.shape[1], TILE - img.shape[2]
        # symmetric, not reflect: reflect cannot pad beyond the array's own size
        # and several of these areas are far smaller than a tile.
        img = np.pad(img, ((0, 0), (0, py), (0, px)), mode="symmetric")
        msk = np.pad(msk, ((0, py), (0, px)), mode="symmetric")
    if augment:
        # Flips and photometric jitter, following the parent study. At 72 crops
        # this is the largest lever available on a network that overfits by the
        # third epoch.
        if np.random.rand() < 0.5:
            img, msk = img[:, :, ::-1], msk[:, ::-1]
        if np.random.rand() < 0.5:
            img, msk = img[:, ::-1, :], msk[::-1, :]
        if np.random.rand() < 0.5:
            k = int(np.random.randint(1, 4))
            img, msk = np.rot90(img, k, (1, 2)), np.rot90(msk, k, (0, 1))
        img = np.clip(img * np.random.uniform(0.9, 1.1)
                      + np.random.uniform(-0.05, 0.05), 0, 1)
    return np.ascontiguousarray(img), np.ascontiguousarray(msk)

# The split, the tile lists and the network's construction sit outside both
# guards below, because the operating point has to be recomputable from a saved
# checkpoint without retraining. Held inside the training guard, as they were,
# the sweep could only run as part of a training run, so a change to the sweep
# cost eight epochs to test. The seed is set before anything draws from the
# generator, and the order of the draws is unchanged, so the trained network is
# the same one this arrangement replaces.
torch.manual_seed(20260812)
areas = sorted(os.path.basename(f)[:-8]
               for f in glob.glob(os.path.join(pair_dir, "*_img.tif")))
val_areas = set(areas[::5])                        # every fifth area held out
trn_areas = [a for a in areas if a not in val_areas]
trn = [t for a in trn_areas for t in index_of(a)]
val = [t for a in sorted(val_areas) for t in index_of(a)]
dev = torch.device("mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")

def build_net():
    """The released seven-channel network with a four-band first layer."""
    net = torch.load(os.path.join(root, "02.inputs", "zwieback-cnn", "model.p"),
                     map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
    old = net.backbone.conv1
    new = nn.Conv2d(4, old.out_channels, old.kernel_size, old.stride,
                    old.padding, bias=False)
    with torch.no_grad():
        new.weight.copy_(old.weight[:, KEEP, :, :])
    net.backbone.conv1 = new
    net.aux_classifier = None                      # COCO head, unused here
    return net.to(dev)

if not (os.path.exists(ckpt) and os.path.exists(metrics_csv)):
    net = build_net().train()
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(
        weight=torch.tensor([1.0, DEAD_W], device=dev))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-4)

    rows, best_iou = [], -1.0
    for ep in range(EPOCHS):
        net.train()
        order = torch.randperm(len(trn)).tolist()
        tot = 0.0
        for i in range(0, len(order), 2):
            b = [load(trn[j], augment=True) for j in order[i:i+2]]
            # An odd tile count leaves one batch of one per epoch, and the ASPP
            # pooling branch reduces it to 1x1, which BatchNorm cannot normalise
            # in training mode. Drop that batch, as a DataLoader's drop_last
            # would. The order is reshuffled every epoch, so no tile is
            # systematically excluded. Without this the chunk runs or crashes
            # according to the parity of the label-pair tile count, which is how
            # it passed at 72 tiles and failed at 79.
            if len(b) < 2:
                continue
            x = torch.tensor(np.stack([t[0] for t in b])).to(dev)
            y = torch.tensor(np.stack([t[1] for t in b])).to(dev)
            opt.zero_grad()
            l = loss_fn(net(x)["out"], y)
            l.backward(); opt.step()
            tot += float(l.detach()) * len(b)
        net.eval()
        tp = fp = fn = 0
        with torch.no_grad():
            for item in val:
                img, msk = load(item)
                x = torch.tensor(img[None]).to(dev)
                p = net(x)["out"].argmax(1)[0].cpu().numpy()
                tp += int(((p == 1) & (msk == 1)).sum())
                fp += int(((p == 1) & (msk == 0)).sum())
                fn += int(((p == 0) & (msk == 1)).sum())
        prec = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0.0
        rec = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0
        iou = tp / (tp + fp + fn) if tp + fp + fn else 0.0
        # Select on IoU rather than on either half of it: recall alone is
        # maximised by flagging everything, precision alone by flagging nothing,
        # and the checkpoint has to be usable as a pre-labeller. Saving the last
        # epoch instead would keep weights that validate worse than an earlier
        # one, which is what the first run of this chunk did.
        saved = iou > best_iou
        if saved:
            best_iou = iou
            torch.save(net.state_dict(), ckpt)
        rows.append(dict(epoch=ep + 1, train_loss=round(tot / len(trn), 4),
                         val_precision=round(prec, 3), val_recall=round(rec, 3),
                         val_iou=round(iou, 3), checkpointed=saved,
                         n_train_tiles=len(trn), n_val_tiles=len(val),
                         n_train_areas=len(trn_areas), n_val_areas=len(val_areas)))
        # Written every epoch, not once at the end, so progress is visible
        # while the loop runs and a later failure cannot discard earlier epochs.
        with open(metrics_csv, "w", newline="") as f:
            w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(rows[0]))
            w.writeheader(); w.writerows(rows)

# Operating point. Pixel precision is not what an annotator experiences: they
# accept or reject candidate polygons, so the threshold is chosen on polygon
# counts after the minimum-area filter, on held-out areas only. Crowns reached
# is counted alongside candidates that hit one, because raising the threshold
# erodes a blob covering several crowns into one piece per crown, which raises
# the count of candidates hitting a crown without reaching a single crown the
# lower threshold missed. Without the second count that erosion reads as a
# gain in precision.
op_csv = os.path.join(root, "03.outputs", "crown_operating_point.csv")
if os.path.exists(ckpt) and not os.path.exists(op_csv):
    import rasterio.features
    from shapely.geometry import shape
    net = build_net()
    net.load_state_dict(torch.load(ckpt, map_location=dev))
    net.eval()
    GSD, MIN_CROWN_M2 = 0.5, 1.0
    sweep = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        probs = []
        for item in val:
            img, msk = load(item)
            p = torch.softmax(net(torch.tensor(img[None]).to(dev))["out"], 1)
            probs.append((p[0, 1].cpu().numpy(), msk))
    # The sweep runs down to 0.1 because crown recall was still rising at the
    # lowest threshold first measured, so 0.3 was the edge of the sweep rather
    # than a best point. One set of probability maps serves every threshold, so
    # the extra rows cost polygonisation alone.
    for thr in [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]:
        n_cand = n_hit = n_true = n_reached = 0
        cand_area = scored_area = 0.0
        for pr, msk in probs:
            binmask = (pr >= thr).astype(np.uint8)
            polys = [(shape(g), v) for g, v in
                     rasterio.features.shapes(binmask, mask=binmask == 1)]
            keep = [g for g, _ in polys if g.area * GSD * GSD >= MIN_CROWN_M2]
            truth = [shape(g) for g, v in
                     rasterio.features.shapes(msk.astype(np.uint8),
                                              mask=msk.astype(np.uint8) == 1)]
            n_cand += len(keep); n_true += len(truth)
            n_hit += sum(1 for g in keep if any(g.intersects(t) for t in truth))
            n_reached += sum(1 for t in truth if any(g.intersects(t)
                                                     for g in keep))
            # Candidate area, not candidate count, is what an annotator works
            # through once the mask merges. At a low threshold the polygon
            # count falls while coverage rises, because separate crowns join
            # into one blob, and a blob covering forty crowns is not one
            # decision.
            cand_area += sum(g.area for g in keep) * GSD * GSD
            scored_area += msk.size * GSD * GSD
        sweep.append(dict(threshold=thr, candidates=n_cand,
                          candidates_hitting_a_crown=n_hit,
                          reference_crowns=n_true,
                          crowns_reached=n_reached,
                          polygon_precision=round(n_hit / n_cand, 3) if n_cand else 0.0,
                          crown_recall=round(n_reached / n_true, 3) if n_true else 0.0,
                          crowns_per_candidate=round(n_reached / n_cand, 1)
                          if n_cand else 0.0,
                          area_flagged=round(cand_area / scored_area, 3)
                          if scored_area else 0.0,
                          candidates_per_km2=round(
                              n_cand / (len(val) * (TILE * GSD) ** 2 / 1e6), 1)))
    with open(op_csv, "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=list(sweep[0]))
        w.writeheader(); w.writerows(sweep)
```

```{r}
                              "crown_net_metrics.csv"))
```

```{r}
#| label: crown-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
best <- crown_m[which.max(crown_m$val_iou), ]
```

Per-epoch figures are in Table S2. Tuning used `r crown_m$n_train_tiles[1]` crops from `r crown_m$n_train_areas[1]` areas against `r crown_m$n_val_tiles[1]` crops from `r crown_m$n_val_areas[1]` held-out areas. The retained network is the one that validates best, epoch `r best$epoch` of `r max(crown_m$epoch)` trained, at a recall of `r sprintf("%.2f", best$val_recall)` and a precision of `r sprintf("%.2f", best$val_precision)`. `r if (best$epoch == max(crown_m$epoch)) "Validation intersection over union was still rising when the schedule ended, so the length of the run bounds the network rather than the network having converged." else "Validation intersection over union falls after that epoch while the training loss keeps falling, so the schedule already runs past its useful length."` For a pre-labeller feeding human triage the operating direction is nonetheless deliberate, because an annotator rejects a false candidate in one action, whereas a crown the network never proposes is never reviewed, and the twenty-to-one class weighting is what buys that recall. These are pixel-wise figures, so the precision an annotator experiences depends on candidate polygons after cleaning rather than on this number directly.

```{r}
#| label: operating-point-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
op <- read.csv(file.path(dirname(inputs), "03.outputs",
                         "crown_operating_point.csv"))
# The block count and the area they cover are read from the committed sample
# rather than typed, so the conversion below cannot drift from the sample.
blk_area <- sf::st_read(file.path(inputs, "derived", "sample_blocks.gpkg"),
                        quiet = TRUE)
blk_km2 <- sum(as.numeric(sf::st_area(blk_area))) / 1e6
```

The full sweep is in Table S3. The queue was generated at the threshold that keeps candidates per square kilometre within what one annotator can work through, not at the threshold that maximises any statistic. The counts above convert directly, since the `r nrow(blk_area)` blocks cover `r sprintf("%.1f", blk_km2)` km² per mosaic epoch, so a rate of `r sprintf("%.0f", op$candidates_per_km2[op$threshold == 0.5])` candidates per square kilometre at a probability threshold of 0.5 implies roughly `r format(round(op$candidates_per_km2[op$threshold == 0.5] * blk_km2), big.mark = ",")` candidates per epoch to review. Polygon precision and crown recall move in opposite directions across the sweep, precision from `r sprintf("%.2f", op$polygon_precision[op$threshold == 0.3])` at a threshold of 0.3 to `r sprintf("%.2f", op$polygon_precision[op$threshold == 0.7])` at 0.7 while the share of delineated crowns reached by any candidate falls from `r sprintf("%.2f", op$crown_recall[op$threshold == 0.3])` to `r sprintf("%.2f", op$crown_recall[op$threshold == 0.7])`, because a higher threshold erodes one candidate covering many crowns into one candidate per crown rather than reaching crowns the lower threshold missed. Precision read alone therefore rewards the threshold that finds fewest crowns. Crown recall keeps rising as the threshold falls, to `r sprintf("%.2f", op$crown_recall[op$threshold == 0.1])` at 0.1, but a candidate stops being one crown well before that, holding `r sprintf("%.1f", op$crowns_per_candidate[op$threshold == 0.1])` crowns at 0.1 and `r sprintf("%.1f", op$crowns_per_candidate[op$threshold == 0.5])` at 0.5, and flagging `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * op$area_flagged[op$threshold == 0.1])` per cent of the scored area against `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * op$area_flagged[op$threshold == 0.5])` per cent. A candidate an annotator accepts or rejects in one action has to be one crown, so the usable range ends near 0.3, where recall is `r sprintf("%.2f", op$crown_recall[op$threshold == 0.3])` and each candidate holds `r sprintf("%.1f", op$crowns_per_candidate[op$threshold == 0.3])` crowns. At that point four crowns in ten are never proposed for review, which is a limit of the network rather than of the threshold, and it bounds what the pre-labeller can save an annotator.

@fig-crownnet draws both, since the tuning trajectory and the operating point are the two things the annotation plan rests on and each currently lives only as a supplement table.

```{r}
#| label: fig-crownnet
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The crown network as tuned and as operated. (a) Precision, recall and intersection over union on held-out delineation areas after each epoch, with the retained epoch marked; the network is kept on intersection over union rather than on either half of it, because recall alone is maximised by flagging everything. (b) The operating-point sweep, showing the share of delineated crowns reached by at least one candidate against the number of crowns each candidate holds. A candidate an annotator accepts or rejects in one action has to be about one crown, so the usable range is bounded on the left by candidates that merge many crowns and on the right by crowns that are never proposed."
#| fig-width: 7

               each = nrow(crown_m)),

           label = "retained", size = 2.4, hjust = 1.15, colour = "grey30") +

  scale_x_continuous(breaks = crown_m$epoch) +
  labs(title = "(a) Fine-tuning", x = "Epoch", y = NULL) +
  th + theme(legend.position = "bottom",
             legend.key.size = unit(.3, "cm"))

opp <- op[op$candidates > 0, ]
pb <- ggplot(opp, aes(crowns_per_candidate, crown_recall)) +

  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", threshold)),
                           size = 2.4, colour = "grey25", seed = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = max(opp$crown_recall) * .5,
           label = "one crown per candidate", size = 2.4, angle = 90,
           vjust = -0.5, colour = "grey30") +
```
