
## Analysis cube

The annual composites were reorganised into a local data cube for the sits package for satellite image time series analysis [@Simoes_2021], which supplies the TempCNN implementation and the tuning, validation and uncertainty tooling used in the modelling sections, and whose local cube convention the radar record follows. A sits cube is a directory of single-band files named by satellite, sensor, tile, band and date. Each composite was split into its four spectral bands under the labels B04, B08, B11 and B12, one nominal date of 1 August per year, Landsat for the 2014 to 2018 baseline and Sentinel-2 from 2019 as pre-registered. The Landsat years carried the same collection labels as the Sentinel-2 years because a cube admits a single collection; bands were harmonized across sensors as described above, and the sensor of origin remains recoverable from the year. The cube's inventory and its checks are in Table S6. Files are rebuilt whenever their source composite changes, and the cube was validated by loading it and checking its timeline and band set. The cube is retained because the measurements below were made on it and because its grid is the grid the radar cells nest in, three to a cell, so the severity labels join both records without resampling.

```{r}
#| label: sits-cube-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
cube_dir <- file.path(inputs, "derived", "sits_cube")
dir.create(cube_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
srcs <- file.path(comp_dir, c(sprintf("ls_%d.tif", 2014:2018),
                              sprintf("s2_%d.tif", 2019:2025)))
if (all(file.exists(srcs))) {
  band_map <- c(red = "B04", nir = "B08", swir16 = "B11", swir22 = "B12")
  wanted <- character(0)
  for (s in srcs) {
    yr <- sub("^\\w+_(\\d{4})\\.tif$", "\\1", basename(s))
    for (b in names(band_map)) {
      f <- file.path(cube_dir,
                     sprintf("SENTINEL-2_MSI_TBL01_%s_%s-08-01.tif",
                             band_map[[b]], yr))
      wanted <- c(wanted, f)
      if (file.exists(f) && file.mtime(f) > file.mtime(s)) next
      writeRaster(rast(s)[[b]], f, overwrite = TRUE,
                  gdal = "COMPRESS=DEFLATE")
    }
  }
  # The chunk owns this directory: anything it did not just write is stale,
  # from an earlier grid or an earlier naming, and would corrupt the timeline.
  unlink(setdiff(list.files(cube_dir, full.names = TRUE), wanted),
         recursive = TRUE)
}
```

The cube was then loaded and checked. The register of those checks is Table S9. The checks were reported rather than suppressed, because a guard whose failure is invisible is not a guard, and an earlier build of this cube passed a silent assertion while holding files from two different grids under malformed dates.

```{r}
#| label: cube-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
library(sits)
cube <- sits_cube(source = "MPC", collection = "SENTINEL-2-L2A",
                  data_dir = cube_dir,
                  parse_info = c("X1", "X2", "tile", "band", "date"),
                  progress = FALSE)
tl <- sits_timeline(cube)
yrs <- as.integer(format(tl, "%Y"))
cube_r <- rast(file.path(cube_dir, "SENTINEL-2_MSI_TBL01_B04_2014-08-01.tif"))
src_r <- rast(file.path(comp_dir, "ls_2014.tif"))
checks <- data.frame(
  property = c("files", "dates", "span", "bands", "tiles", "cells",
               "extent equals source"),
  value = c(length(list.files(cube_dir)),
            length(tl),
            paste(format(min(tl)), "to", format(max(tl))),
            paste(sort(sits_bands(cube)), collapse = " "),
            nrow(cube),
            paste(dim(cube_r)[1:2], collapse = " x "),
            isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(ext(cube_r)), as.vector(ext(src_r))))),
  passes = c(length(list.files(cube_dir)) == 4 * length(tl),
             length(tl) == length(srcs),
             all(diff(yrs) == 1) && !any(yrs < 1900 | yrs > 2100),
             identical(sort(sits_bands(cube)), c("B04", "B08", "B11", "B12")),
             nrow(cube) == 1,
             identical(dim(cube_r)[1:2], dim(src_r)[1:2]),
             isTRUE(all.equal(as.vector(ext(cube_r)), as.vector(ext(src_r))))))
stopifnot(all(checks$passes))
```

@fig-trajectory shows what the cube holds, the annual reflectance of the sampled blocks across the whole record, so the outbreak years can be read against the pre-outbreak baseline the optical design differenced them from. It also shows the discontinuity that set the record aside.

```{r}
#| label: trajectory-build
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# One mean per block per band per year, extracted once and written, because
# reading forty-eight rasters of 2385 by 2023 cells on this machine is the
# expensive part and nothing about it changes between renders.
traj_f <- file.path(root, "03.outputs", "block_trajectories.csv")
if (!file.exists(traj_f)) {
  blk_t <- sf::st_read(file.path(inputs, "derived", "sample_blocks.gpkg"),
                       quiet = TRUE)
  blk_t$block <- seq_len(nrow(blk_t))
  cube_files <- list.files(file.path(inputs, "derived", "sits_cube"),
                           pattern = "^SENTINEL.*\\.tif$", full.names = TRUE)
  rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(cube_files, function(f) {
    parts <- strsplit(basename(f), "_")[[1]]
    band <- parts[4]
    year <- as.integer(substr(parts[5], 1, 4))
    v <- terra::extract(terra::rast(f), terra::vect(blk_t), fun = mean,
                        na.rm = TRUE, ID = FALSE)
    data.frame(block = blk_t$block, band = band, year = year,
               value = as.numeric(v[, 1]))
  }))
  write.csv(rows, traj_f, row.names = FALSE)
}
traj <- read.csv(traj_f)
```

```{r}
#| label: trajectory-step
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The size of the year-to-year step at the sensor boundary against the size of
# every other step in the series, per band. If the boundary step is the largest
# in the record, the harmonisation has not removed it and the two-window
# difference the baseline computes straddles it.
step_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(traj, traj$band), function(d) {
  m <- aggregate(value ~ year, d, median)
  m <- m[order(m$year), ]
  st <- diff(m$value)
  yrs <- m$year[-1]
  data.frame(band = d$band[1], boundary = st[yrs == 2019],
             other_median = median(abs(st[yrs != 2019])),
             ratio = abs(st[yrs == 2019]) / median(abs(st[yrs != 2019])))
}))
```

The step between 2018 and 2019 was the sensor boundary, where the record changed from Landsat 8 to Sentinel-2, and the harmonisation had not removed it. In shortwave infrared 2 that step is `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_tab$boundary[step_tab$band == "B12"])` reflectance against a median absolute step of `r sprintf("%.4f", step_tab$other_median[step_tab$band == "B12"])` across every other year in the record, a ratio of `r sprintf("%.1f", step_tab$ratio[step_tab$band == "B12"])`, and in shortwave infrared 1 the ratio is `r sprintf("%.1f", step_tab$ratio[step_tab$band == "B11"])`. In both bands the boundary was the largest single step in twelve years. This bears directly on the pre-registered baseline, which differences the 2019 to 2021 mean against the 2014 to 2016 mean and therefore straddles the boundary, so part of what that difference measures is the sensor rather than the stand. The direction compounds the problem, since the step raises post-outbreak shortwave infrared, which is the direction mortality moves it. A step of this kind is what the published cross-sensor coefficients exist to remove [@Zhang_2018; @Chastain_2019], and what the Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 product applies as a matter of course [@Claverie_2018; @Ju_2025]; neither was applied to this cube, whose harmonisation follows the band mapping of @Perbet_2024 alone. The size of the effect was measured here rather than assumed, and the amendment of 2026-09-09 answered it by moving the predictor record to radar rather than by correcting the join.

```{r}
#| label: step-by-damage
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Whether the step is the sensor or the stand, tested without any published
# coefficient, because the two papers carrying those coefficients could not be
# retrieved. If the step is the sensor it is the same in blocks the aerial
# survey never recorded damage in as in blocks it did. The damage flag is the
# survey-based stratification variable, not a severity value, so this touches
# no severity raster.
blk_d <- sf::st_read(file.path(inputs, "derived", "sample_blocks.gpkg"),
                     quiet = TRUE)
blk_d <- data.frame(block = seq_len(nrow(blk_d)), damage = blk_d$damage)
step_blk <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(traj, list(traj$block, traj$band)),
  function(d) {
    d <- d[order(d$year), ]
    i <- which(d$year == 2019)
    if (!length(i) || i == 1) return(NULL)
    data.frame(block = d$block[1], band = d$band[1],
               step = d$value[i] - d$value[i - 1])
  }))
step_blk <- merge(step_blk, blk_d, by = "block")
# A block with no clear observation in either year has no step to compare, so
# it is dropped here and the counts reported are the blocks actually used.
step_blk <- step_blk[!is.na(step_blk$step), ]
step_test <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(step_blk, step_blk$band), function(d) {
  a <- d$step[d$damage]; b <- d$step[!d$damage]
  w <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(a, b))
  data.frame(band = d$band[1],
             med_damage = median(a), iqr_damage = IQR(a),
             med_none = median(b), iqr_none = IQR(b),
             n_damage = length(a), n_none = length(b),
             W = unname(w$statistic), p = w$p.value)
}))
```

The step was the sensor rather than the stand, on the evidence available here. Across the `r step_test$n_damage[1]` blocks in which the aerial survey recorded damage the median 2018 to 2019 step in shortwave infrared 2 was `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_test$med_damage[step_test$band == "B12"])` reflectance, against `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_test$med_none[step_test$band == "B12"])` across the `r step_test$n_none[1]` blocks in which it recorded none, a difference no rank-sum test distinguishes \[W = `r sprintf("%.0f", step_test$W[step_test$band == "B12"])`, p = `r sprintf("%.2f", step_test$p[step_test$band == "B12"])`\]. Shortwave infrared 1 behaves the same way, `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_test$med_damage[step_test$band == "B11"])` against `r sprintf("%+.4f", step_test$med_none[step_test$band == "B11"])` \[W = `r sprintf("%.0f", step_test$W[step_test$band == "B11"])`, p = `r sprintf("%.2f", step_test$p[step_test$band == "B11"])`\]. A step of the same size in stands with no recorded mortality as in stands with it is an instrument boundary rather than an outbreak, and in both shortwave-infrared bands the undamaged blocks moved slightly further than the damaged ones, which is the opposite of what mortality would produce. The two visible and near-infrared bands do separate the groups weakly, red at p = `r sprintf("%.2f", step_test$p[step_test$band == "B04"])` and near infrared at p = `r sprintf("%.2f", step_test$p[step_test$band == "B08"])`, so the boundary is not purely instrumental everywhere in the spectrum; it is instrumental in the two bands the detectability floor rests on. This was tested without applying any published cross-sensor coefficient, because neither of the two papers carrying those coefficients could be retrieved through an open repository, and the survey damage flag used here is the stratification variable rather than a severity value. With the step shown to be the instrument and the pre-outbreak window shown to be thin, the optical record was set aside as a predictor and the radar record took its place; the three options weighed, a corrected two-sensor record, a Landsat-only record and radar, are recorded with their measurements in the sensor design decision cited above.

```{r}
#| label: fig-trajectory
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Annual surface reflectance of the 160 sampled blocks across the analysis cube, 2014 to 2025, one panel per band. The line is the median block and the ribbon the interquartile range, so the spread is the between-block variation the models have to work in rather than a measurement error. Years 2014 to 2018 are Landsat 8 and 2019 onward Sentinel-2, and the step between those two years is the sensor boundary rather than the outbreak, which the text quantifies. The dashed line marks the 2016 outbreak onset."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
band_lab <- c(B04 = "B04, red", B08 = "B08, near infrared",
              B11 = "B11, shortwave infrared 1",
              B12 = "B12, shortwave infrared 2")
tr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(traj, list(traj$band, traj$year)),
  function(d) data.frame(
    band = d$band[1], year = d$year[1],
    med = median(d$value, na.rm = TRUE),
    lo = quantile(d$value, .25, na.rm = TRUE),
    hi = quantile(d$value, .75, na.rm = TRUE))))
tr$band <- factor(band_lab[tr$band], levels = band_lab)

ggplot(tr, aes(year, med)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "steelblue4", alpha = .22) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2016, linetype = "22", colour = "grey30") +
  geom_line(linewidth = .55, colour = "steelblue4") +
  geom_point(size = .8, colour = "steelblue4") +
  facet_wrap(~ band, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2014, 2024, 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Surface reflectance") + th
```

## Subsequence sampling

Following @Perbet_2024, the record is cut into fixed-length subsequences rather than modelled as one full series, and on the monthly radar record a subsequence spans months rather than years. The pre-registration fixed subsequences of seven to ten years on an annual record, and the span on the monthly record is fixed by the amendment of 2026-09-09 rather than here. For labelled stands the mortality-onset date is placed at a randomized position within the window (never the first step) as augmentation, so models learn the trajectory shape rather than a calendar position, a positional augmentation of the kind surveyed for time series classification by @Iwana_2021. Subsequences are drawn so that every labelled stand is observed from the June 2017 start of the radar record through the present. There is no pre-outbreak radar state, because the outbreak began about 2016 and the dual-polarisation record in 2017, so the models recognise the trajectory of a stand rather than its change from a baseline, which is what a temporal convolutional network is for and what @Hechtl_2025 did. Each labelled stand cell contributes its severity fraction, its onset interval from cross-epoch triangulation, and the climate values fitted at the same monthly step. Onset supervision is interval-censored, so the dating loss credits any predicted onset falling within a stand's bracket rather than forcing an arbitrary point label. Undisturbed stands, drawn from surveyed-absence areas outside recorded damage, complete the training set.

@fig-design draws the sampling scheme and the two-head design together, as pre-registered on the annual record, since neither is legible from prose alone; the monthly record changes the step and not the scheme.

```{r}
#| label: fig-design
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The subsequence sampling scheme and the two-head design, both as pre-registered. (a) The annual record 2014 to 2025 is cut into fixed-length subsequences of seven to ten years, four of which are drawn as examples; the onset year sits at a randomised position inside each window and never at its first year, so the network learns the shape of the trajectory rather than a calendar position. The shaded band is the censoring interval for a stand alive at the 2020 label epoch and dead by the 2023 one; a stand already dead in 2020 carries an open bracket before that epoch instead, which is the case for the first and third subsequences drawn. (b) One convolutional trunk over the temporal axis feeds two heads, severity and relative onset year, and the onset head is scored against the bracket rather than a point, which is the loss H2 is defined by."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.2
yrs <- 2014:2025
win <- data.frame(id = factor(1:4), start = c(2014, 2016, 2015, 2018),
                  len = c(8, 10, 7, 8), onset = c(2018, 2021, 2019, 2022))
win$end <- win$start + win$len - 1
pa <- ggplot(win) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2020, xmax = 2023, ymin = 0.4, ymax = 4.6,
           fill = "grey88") +
  annotate("text", x = 2021.5, y = 4.85, label = "censoring bracket",
           size = 2.5, colour = "grey25") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = start, xend = end, y = as.numeric(id),
                   yend = as.numeric(id)), linewidth = 3.2,
               colour = "steelblue4", alpha = .8, lineend = "round") +
  geom_point(aes(x = onset, y = as.numeric(id)), size = 2.1,
             colour = "#C0392B") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = yrs, limits = c(2013.6, 2025.4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:4, labels = paste("subsequence", 1:4),
                     limits = c(0.4, 5.1)) +
  labs(title = "(a) Subsequence sampling", x = NULL, y = NULL) + th

box <- data.frame(
  x = c(1, 2.35, 3.7, 5.05, 5.05),
  y = c(3, 3, 3, 3.8, 2.2),
  lab = c("input\n7 to 10 years\nx 4 bands +\n3 climate", "temporal\nconvolutions",
          "dense\nlayers", "severity\nhead", "onset\nhead"))
seg <- data.frame(x = c(1.5, 2.85, 4.2, 4.2), xend = c(1.85, 3.2, 4.55, 4.55),
                  y = c(3, 3, 3, 3), yend = c(3, 3, 3.8, 2.2))
pb <- ggplot() +
  geom_tile(data = box, aes(x, y), width = 1.0, height = 1.05,
            fill = "grey95", colour = "grey45", linewidth = .3) +
  geom_text(data = box, aes(x, y, label = lab), size = 2.4, lineheight = .95) +
  geom_segment(data = seg, aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = yend),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(.14, "cm")), linewidth = .35,
               colour = "grey35") +
  annotate("text", x = 5.05, y = 1.45,
           label = "scored against the bracket, not a point",
           size = 2.3, colour = "#C0392B") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0.4, 5.75)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1.2, 4.5)) +
  labs(title = "(b) Two-head design", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  th + theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank(),
             panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.border = element_blank())

pa / pb + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.15))
```

## Architectures

Two deep learning networks are applied to the time series, following the comparative design of @Perbet_2024. Both take the same input series, the monthly K0 and K1 elements of the radar record with the climate values fitted at the same step. TempCNN applies one-dimensional convolutions along the temporal axis of a satellite time series, learning discriminative temporal features without handcrafted metrics; convolutional layers are applied to the temporal sequence without pooling, which degrades performance in this setting [@Pelletier_2019], followed by fully connected layers and task heads. The Transformer encoder classifies sequences through self-attention, weighting every observation of the series against every other and thereby capturing long-range temporal dependencies without recurrence [@Ru_wurm_2020]; for sequence-to-label tasks only the encoder stack is required, multi-head attention blocks followed by feed-forward layers. In boreal disturbance classification TempCNN matched or exceeded a LandTrendr-plus-random-forest workflow, with its largest margins on partial disturbance classes, and the Transformer performed within two accuracy points of it [@Perbet_2024]; both architectures are retained because their attention patterns differ instructively on gradual disturbances. Transformers over Sentinel-2 have since been applied to forest disturbance in Central Europe [@Schiller_2024], and the deep learning literature on satellite image time series has accumulated recurrent detectors [@Kong_2018], attention over a convolutional trunk [@Tang_2022] and self-supervised pretraining against label scarcity [@Yuan_2021], reviewed by @Miller_2024.

## Baseline model

The comparator for the first hypothesis was restated by the amendment of 2026-09-09, which stands unsigned. The pre-registered null model reproduced the stand-scale change analysis that defines the current detection floor [@Zwieback_2024], a difference of pre-outbreak and post-outbreak summer mean reflectance per stand cell in the SWIR band, with the normalized burn ratio family it anchors [@Kennedy_2010; @Cohen_2017], fitted as a calibrated univariate model on training folds only. That difference cannot be formed on a record that begins after the outbreak did, since there is no pre-outbreak radar state and there cannot be one. The comparator therefore becomes the published floor itself, the severity of 0.1 above which @Zwieback_2024 found stand-scale SWIR change related clearly to severity, which is the quantity the study's title claims to lower and the quantity the field currently accepts, rather than a reimplementation of the change analysis on a contaminated optical record. Two alternatives were weighed and rejected, a radar change baseline, which needs a pre-outbreak radar state that does not exist, and a single-date radar classifier, which would test the value of the time series rather than the floor. SWIR change is the strongest single-band signal for beetle-killed spruce at Landsat scale but relates clearly to severity only above 0.1 [@Zwieback_2024], and index-based methods generally weaken on partial and gradual disturbance [@Cohen_2017; @Senf_2017]. The published state of the art for the same task is the annual random forest mapping of @Bright_2020, which trains on high-resolution crowns aggregated to percent-dead at 30 m and enters here as a comparator rather than the method, and dense-time-series work has recovered subtle change in both mountain pine beetle and spruce beetle systems [@Ye_2021].

## Model training

TempCNN and the Transformer encoder are trained on identical inputs, the monthly K0 and K1 series with the climate values fitted at the same step, with two heads, a severity output, classified at the pre-registered breaks with the continuous fraction retained for regression reporting, and a relative onset output. Both networks are implemented through the sits package [@Simoes_2021] on its torch backend, which also supplies the tuning, validation and uncertainty tools applied below. Architectures follow @Pelletier_2019 and @Perbet_2024; optimisation uses Adam with cross-entropy losses, dropout and weight decay, with hyperparameters tuned on a validation split held apart from all test blocks. The onset head is a discrete-time formulation over the censoring bracket, following the neural discrete-time survival model of @Gensheimer_2019, which is what allows an interval label to be scored without inventing a point within it; on the monthly record the bracket is finer and the loss is unchanged. Ablation variants for the second and third hypotheses retrain the identical architecture with, respectively, point onset labels in place of intervals, and the climate values removed. Exact architecture depths, loss weights and schedules are fixed at pre-registration and the subsequence span on the monthly record by its amendment; training runs on cloud graphics hardware with configurations and logs archived alongside the analysis code.

## Endmember calibration

The synthetic test below stands or falls on one quantity, how much a stand's reflectance moves per unit of dead-crown area. Assuming that quantity would make the test circular, because a small assumed contrast guarantees that low severities are unrecoverable. It was therefore measured, from the published crown delineations rather than from any severity product. Within each delineation area the crowns were rasterised to the 90 m stand grid as the fraction of each cell they cover, giving an observed areal severity that depends on no model. Composite reflectance for the same cells was then regressed on that fraction, band by band, at the 2021 growing season the crowns were delineated in. Under linear areal mixing the intercept estimates the live stand spectrum and the slope estimates the difference between a fully dead and a fully live stand, which is exactly the endmember the simulation needs.

Two limits were stated rather than buried. The delineation areas fall inside the reference footprint held out as fold 8, so this uses fold-8 imagery to fix a simulation parameter; it was treated as a pilot calculation, declared as such, and no fold-8 cell enters model training. The areas were also selected for crown density, so they sample the severity range unrepresentatively, which biases the range covered but not the per-unit contrast being estimated.

```{r}
#| label: endmember-calibration
#| echo: true
#| output: false
em_csv <- file.path(dirname(inputs), "03.outputs", "endmember.csv")
if (!file.exists(em_csv)) {
  library(sf)
  BANDS4 <- c("red", "nir", "swir16", "swir22")
  post <- rast(file.path(comp_dir, "s2_2021.tif"))[[BANDS4]]
  # The simulation offsets each cell from its OWN live spectrum, so the quantity
  # to estimate is the change per unit severity, not the between-cell contrast
  # at one date. Regressing levels estimates a different and far noisier thing:
  # it asks whether cells that hold more dead crowns look different from cells
  # that do not, which stand type, slope and shadow dominate. Differencing
  # against a pre-outbreak baseline removes every stable per-cell difference.
  # The baseline is Landsat and the post state Sentinel-2, so a cross-sensor
  # offset enters; it is common to all cells and lands in the intercept, leaving
  # the slope on severity identifiable.
  pre <- mean(rast(file.path(comp_dir, "ls_2014.tif"))[[BANDS4]],
              rast(file.path(comp_dir, "ls_2015.tif"))[[BANDS4]])
  grid <- c(post, post - pre)     # levels first, then the post minus pre change
  names(grid) <- c(BANDS4, paste0("d_", BANDS4))
  cells <- list()
  for (f in lab_f) {
    l <- suppressWarnings(st_read(f, quiet = TRUE))
    if (nrow(l) == 0) next
    if (!identical(st_crs(l)$epsg, 32605L)) {
      if (suppressWarnings(st_bbox(l))[["xmin"]] > 1000) l <- st_set_crs(l, 32605)
    }
    g <- crop(grid, ext(vect(l)) + 180, snap = "out")
    if (ncell(g) < 4) next
    # cover = TRUE gives the fraction of each 90 m cell inside a crown polygon,
    # which is areal severity measured directly, with no model in between.
    fr <- rasterize(vect(l), g[[1]], cover = TRUE, background = 0)
    d <- data.frame(sev = values(fr)[, 1], values(g))
    cells[[basename(f)]] <- d[is.finite(d$sev) & complete.cases(d), ]
  }
  cd <- do.call(rbind, cells)
  cd <- cd[cd$red > 0 & cd$nir > 0, ]
  fit1 <- function(y, b, est) {
    m <- lm(y ~ cd$sev)
    ci <- confint(m)[2, ]
    data.frame(estimator = est, band = b,
               intercept = round(coef(m)[[1]], 4),
               endmember = round(coef(m)[[2]], 4),
               ci_low = round(ci[[1]], 4), ci_high = round(ci[[2]], 4),
               r2 = round(summary(m)$r.squared, 4))
  }
  em <- rbind(
    do.call(rbind, lapply(BANDS4, function(b) fit1(cd[[b]], b, "level"))),
    do.call(rbind, lapply(BANDS4, function(b)
      fit1(cd[[paste0("d_", b)]], b, "change"))))
  em$n_cells <- nrow(cd)
  em$max_sev <- round(max(cd$sev), 3)
  write.csv(em, em_csv, row.names = FALSE)
}
endmember_tbl <- read.csv(em_csv)
```

```{r}
#| label: em-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
emv <- function(est, b, col = "endmember")
  endmember_tbl[[col]][endmember_tbl$estimator == est & endmember_tbl$band == b]
```

```{r}
#| label: endmember-assumed
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# The endmember assumed before anything was measured, defined here rather than
# inside the guarded block below so the prose can read it instead of repeating
# the number. A figure typed twice is a figure that drifts once.
EM_ASSUMED <- c(red = 0.040, nir = -0.060, swir16 = 0.055, swir22 = 0.045)
```

Both estimators are reported in Table S7. The estimate covers `r endmember_tbl$n_cells[1]` stand cells reaching a maximum observed dead-crown fraction of `r endmember_tbl$max_sev[1]`. The two estimators answer different questions and only the second answers the one that matters. Regressing levels asks whether cells holding more dead crowns look different from cells holding none, a comparison that stand composition, slope and canopy shadow dominate; it returns an R² of `r sprintf("%.3f", emv("level", "swir16", "r2"))` in the shortwave infrared and a slope of the wrong sign, which is a statement about between-cell confounding rather than about mortality. Differencing each cell against its own pre-outbreak state removes those stable differences and estimates the quantity the mixing model actually defines. The change estimator puts the shortwave-infrared endmember at `r sprintf("%+.3f", emv("change", "swir16"))` with a 95 percent interval of `r sprintf("%+.3f to %+.3f", emv("change", "swir16", "ci_low"), emv("change", "swir16", "ci_high"))`, against the `r sprintf("%+.3f", EM_ASSUMED[["swir16"]])` assumed before measurement. The synthetic test below was run at both values so the consequence of the assumption is visible rather than asserted.

Three properties of this estimate constrain how far it can be pushed. The measured shortwave-infrared contrast is roughly two and a half times the assumed one, so the assumption was conservative and the detectability question is correspondingly more open than the first synthetic run implied. Severity nonetheless explains very little of the variance, with R² between `r sprintf("%.3f", min(endmember_tbl$r2[endmember_tbl$estimator == "change"]))` and `r sprintf("%.3f", max(endmember_tbl$r2[endmember_tbl$estimator == "change"]))`, so these are weak slopes estimated over many cells rather than a tight relationship; all four intervals nonetheless exclude zero. The near-infrared slope is positive in addition, at `r sprintf("%+.3f", emv("change", "nir"))`, where dead foliage at crown scale lowers near-infrared reflectance [@Zwieback_2024]. Two readings are available and this design cannot separate them, since canopy loss over a five-year window admits understory response that raises stand near-infrared even as individual crowns darken, or the Landsat baseline and Sentinel-2 post state differ in near-infrared band pass in a way that a common intercept does not absorb. The synthetic test uses the measured vector as estimated, sign included, because substituting the expected sign would reintroduce exactly the assumption this section exists to remove.

## Pipeline validation

Before any labelled data reach the models, the pipeline was tested against a signal whose truth is known because this manuscript injects it. Real trajectories were drawn from the analysis cube, so phenology, atmosphere and sensor noise were those of the study area; only the disturbance was synthetic. Mortality was added as linear areal mixing, the observed spectrum becoming the severity-weighted mix of that cell's own live spectrum and a dead-crown endmember, applied from a known onset year and ramped over two years after @Hicke_2024, whose Alaskan *Dendroctonus* fade runs from green through red to gray rather than completing within a season. Two single-band-head models stand in for the pre-registered two-head design until the interval-censored head exists, one classifying the severity stratum and the other the onset year.

Everything the test reports is conditional on the dead-crown endmember, which is an assumption, not a measurement, and is the quantity that decides whether low severities are recoverable at all. At the value used here a severity of 0.05 shifts shortwave-infrared reflectance by `r sprintf("%.4f", 0.05 * EM_ASSUMED[["swir16"]])`, which is smaller than the between-year scatter of the composites themselves. The test therefore measures whether the pipeline can recover a signal of a stated size; it is not evidence about spruce beetle detectability, and no result below bears on H1.

```{r}
#| label: synthetic-validation
#| echo: true
#| output: false
out_dir <- file.path(dirname(inputs), "03.outputs")
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
syn_f <- file.path(out_dir, c("synthetic_severity_recall.csv",
                              "synthetic_onset_summary.csv"))
if (!all(file.exists(syn_f))) {
  set.seed(20260812)
  YEARS <- 2014:2025
  BANDS <- c(B04 = "red", B08 = "nir", B11 = "swir16", B12 = "swir22")
  N_SAMP <- 4000; N_CAND <- 40000
  STRATA <- c(0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 1)   # pre-registered breaks
  ONSETS <- 2017:2023
  # Reflectance offset of a pure dead stand from the live stand spectrum. The
  # first is the value assumed before anything was measured; the second is the
  # regression slope from the crown delineations. Running both is the point:
  # the assumed value alone would make the low-severity result circular.
  emc <- endmember_tbl[endmember_tbl$estimator == "change", ]
  em_m <- setNames(emc$endmember, emc$band)
  ENDMEMBERS <- list(
    assumed = EM_ASSUMED,
    measured = em_m[c("red", "nir", "swir16", "swir22")])

  cf <- function(b, y) file.path(cube_dir,
         sprintf("SENTINEL-2_MSI_TBL01_%s_%d-08-01.tif", b, y))
  cand <- sample(ncell(rast(cf("B04", 2014))), N_CAND)
  arr <- array(NA_real_, c(N_CAND, length(YEARS), length(BANDS)))
  for (bi in seq_along(BANDS)) for (yi in seq_along(YEARS)) {
    arr[, yi, bi] <- rast(cf(names(BANDS)[bi], YEARS[yi]))[cand][, 1]
  }
  ok <- apply(arr, 1, function(m) all(is.finite(m)) && all(m > 0 & m < 1))
  ndvi <- (arr[, 1, 2] - arr[, 1, 1]) / (arr[, 1, 2] + arr[, 1, 1])
  sel <- sample(which(ok & !is.na(ndvi) & ndvi > 0.4), N_SAMP)
  base <- arr[sel, , , drop = FALSE]

  n_dist <- N_SAMP / 2
  grp <- rep(seq_len(length(STRATA) - 1), length.out = n_dist)
  sev <- numeric(N_SAMP); onset <- rep(NA_integer_, N_SAMP)
  for (i in seq_len(n_dist)) {
    lo <- max(STRATA[grp[i]], 1e-3); hi <- STRATA[grp[i] + 1]
    sev[i] <- exp(runif(1, log(lo), log(hi)))
    onset[i] <- sample(ONSETS, 1)
  }
  inject <- function(em) {
    o <- base
    for (i in seq_len(n_dist)) {
      yi <- match(onset[i], YEARS)
      for (k in seq(yi, length(YEARS))) {
        w <- min(1, (k - yi + 1) / 2)        # two-year fade to full contrast
        for (bi in seq_along(BANDS))
          o[i, k, bi] <- base[i, k, bi] + w * sev[i] * em[[bi]]
      }
    }
    pmin(pmax(o, 0), 1)
  }
  sev_class <- as.character(cut(sev, STRATA, include.lowest = TRUE))
  sev_class[sev == 0] <- "none"
  onset_class <- ifelse(is.na(onset), "none", as.character(onset))

  to_sits <- function(x, label) {
    ts <- lapply(seq_len(dim(x)[1]), function(i) {
      d <- data.frame(Index = as.Date(sprintf("%d-08-01", YEARS)))
      for (bi in seq_along(BANDS)) d[[names(BANDS)[bi]]] <- x[i, , bi]
      tibble::as_tibble(d)
    })
    tb <- tibble::tibble(longitude = 0, latitude = 0,
      start_date = as.Date("2014-08-01"), end_date = as.Date("2025-08-01"),
      label = label, cube = "SYNTHETIC", time_series = ts)
    class(tb) <- c("sits", class(tb)); tb
  }
  tr_i <- sample(N_SAMP, floor(0.75 * N_SAMP))
  te_i <- setdiff(seq_len(N_SAMP), tr_i)
  run <- function(obs, labels) {
    m <- sits_train(to_sits(obs[tr_i, , , drop = FALSE], labels[tr_i]),
                    sits_tempcnn(epochs = 60, batch_size = 64,
                                 validation_split = 0.2, verbose = FALSE))
    p <- sits_classify(to_sits(obs[te_i, , , drop = FALSE], labels[te_i]),
                       m, progress = FALSE, multicores = 2)
    data.frame(truth = labels[te_i],
               pred = vapply(p$predicted, function(x) x$class[[1]], character(1)))
  }

  recall_rows <- list(); onset_rows <- list()
  for (tag in names(ENDMEMBERS)) {
    obs <- inject(ENDMEMBERS[[tag]])
    rs <- run(obs, sev_class); ro <- run(obs, onset_class)
    bs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(rs$truth)), function(s) {
      i <- rs$truth == s
      data.frame(endmember = tag, stratum = s, n = sum(i),
                 recall = round(mean(rs$pred[i] == s), 3))
    }))
    bs$overall_accuracy <- round(mean(rs$pred == rs$truth), 3)
    recall_rows[[tag]] <- bs
    d <- ro$truth != "none" & ro$pred != "none"
    err <- abs(as.integer(ro$truth[d]) - as.integer(ro$pred[d]))
    onset_rows[[tag]] <- data.frame(endmember = tag,
      n_disturbed_test = sum(ro$truth != "none"),
      classified_disturbed = sum(d),
      onset_mae_years = ifelse(sum(d) > 0, round(mean(err), 3), NA),
      within_1yr = ifelse(sum(d) > 0, round(mean(err <= 1), 3), NA))
  }
  write.csv(do.call(rbind, recall_rows), syn_f[1], row.names = FALSE)
  write.csv(do.call(rbind, onset_rows), syn_f[2], row.names = FALSE)
}
syn_recall <- read.csv(syn_f[1]); syn_onset <- read.csv(syn_f[2])
```

```{r}
#| label: syn-numbers
#| echo: true
#| output: false
sy <- function(tag) syn_recall[syn_recall$endmember == tag, ]
lo_str <- c("[0,0.01]", "(0.01,0.03]", "(0.03,0.05]", "(0.05,0.1]")
best <- function(tag) { d <- sy(tag); d$stratum[which.max(d$recall)] }
peak <- function(tag) max(sy(tag)$recall)
lowmax <- function(tag) { d <- sy(tag); max(d$recall[d$stratum %in% lo_str]) }
on <- function(tag) syn_onset[syn_onset$endmember == tag, ]
```

Under the endmember assumed before measurement, recovery was confined to the largest stratum. Recall peaked at `r sprintf("%.2f", peak("assumed"))` in the `r best("assumed")` stratum and reached at most `r sprintf("%.2f", lowmax("assumed"))` anywhere below 0.10, while undisturbed cells were returned correctly `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sy("assumed")$recall[sy("assumed")$stratum == "none"])` of the time. Under the measured endmember, recall peaked at `r sprintf("%.2f", peak("measured"))` in the `r best("measured")` stratum and reached `r sprintf("%.2f", lowmax("measured"))` at best below 0.10. Overall accuracy in both cases was carried almost entirely by the undisturbed majority and should not be read on its own. Onset dating was not a skill estimate under either condition, since `r on("assumed")$classified_disturbed` and `r on("measured")$classified_disturbed` of `r on("assumed")$n_disturbed_test` disturbed test samples were classified as disturbed at all, so the associated mean absolute errors describe whichever cases carried the strongest severity signal rather than the population.

Recall by stratum under both endmembers is in Table S8. What this establishes is narrow and worth stating plainly. The cube, the sample assembly, the sits training path and the classification path run end to end and recover a large injected decline together with its date. The comparison between the two endmembers is the informative part, since it separates what follows from an arbitrary choice from what follows from the contrast the delineated crowns actually exhibit. Measuring the contrast rather than assuming it roughly trebles the number of disturbed stands the onset model recognises at all and lifts recall in the 0.1 to 0.2 stratum by more than an order of magnitude, yet leaves the strata below 0.1, which are the strata this study exists to address, essentially unrecovered.

That result should not be read as a forecast of H1, for a reason of construction rather than caution. The test scores a seven-way assignment of severity class, whereas H1 is scored as detection at a fixed operating point of 0.90 precision within a single stratum, a materially easier task that a multiclass error rate does not estimate. The simulation also carries no climate channels, so it cannot speak to H3, and it supervises onset as a bare class rather than through the interval-censored likelihood H2 is defined by. It further assumes one endmember for every stand, where real stands vary, and variation blurs rather than sharpens. What can be said is bounded and still useful before any label exists. On this cube, at the contrast these crowns exhibit, a four-band annual composite carries a weak but non-zero severity signal that a temporal convolutional network converts into skill only above roughly 0.1, and the design's central claim therefore rests on whether the pre-registered detection framing, the climate channels and the interval supervision together recover what multiclass assignment on spectra alone does not.

## Model evaluation

Evaluation uses block spatial cross-validation, with the study area tessellated into large contiguous blocks assigned wholly to folds to limit spatial autocorrelation leakage [@Perbet_2024], the design @Roberts_2017 set out for data with spatial structure and whose absence @Karasiak_2021 showed inflates reported accuracy in remote sensing. Skill is reported per severity stratum. Detection is summarised by full confusion matrices with user's and producer's accuracy per class, following the good practice of @Olofsson_2014 and the issues @Stehman_2019 sets out, with the spatial unit of assessment stated because it changes the estimate [@Stehman_2011]. The kappa coefficient is not reported, on the grounds @Foody_2020 gives for abandoning it and the earlier objections of @Foody_2004 and @Foody_2008 to comparing thematic maps by a single agreement statistic. The primary metric is recall at a fixed precision of 0.90 in the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, because precision and recall describe a rare positive class where a receiver operating characteristic does not [@Saito_2015; @Sofaer_2019]. Severity regression is summarised by root-mean-square error, relative RMSE normalised by the stratum mean of the reference severity, mean absolute error, and Theil's U inequality coefficient with its bias, variance and covariance decomposition, matching and extending the error reporting of @Zwieback_2024; the decomposition separates systematic under- or over-prediction from unexplained scatter, on the same reasoning that recommends decomposing mean squared error rather than reporting it whole [@Gupta_2009; @Hodson_2021]. Onset dating is summarised by mean absolute error in years. All metrics are reported with fold-wise dispersion. Hypothesis tests are paired and fold-wise, a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank on the primary metric difference with a block-bootstrap confidence interval, the non-parametric paired comparison @Demsar_2006 recommends for classifiers evaluated over a common set of partitions, supported by McNemar's test on paired cell-level detections, which @Dietterich_1998 found to hold its size where resampled t-tests do not. The detectability floor of each method is the lowest severity stratum in which detection skill exceeds the pre-registered threshold, and H1 is tested by paired comparison of deep and baseline skill across folds within the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum. H2 is tested by an ablation in which the same architectures are retrained with single-epoch labels in place of triangulated onset intervals, compared fold-wise on onset mean absolute error. H3 is tested by the equivalent ablation on inputs, climate-augmented against spectral-only models, compared fold-wise on the primary detection metric. The three confirmatory tests form one Holm-corrected family. The severity product of @Zwieback_2024 provides a fully independent evaluation in the Talkeetna to Byers Lake footprint. Because the published crown labels of that study now participate in training, this evaluation uses only fold models whose training blocks exclude the footprint entirely. The reconstructed annual outbreak progression is evaluated separately by areal correspondence with annual aerial survey extent, following the map-scale comparison of @Perbet_2024 and the historical disturbance record its authors subsequently released [@Perbet_2025], and is reported as descriptive rather than confirmatory. Confusion matrices, class balances and validation support are reported in full [after @Hicke_2024].

```{r}
#| label: planned-severity-strata
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
# Activated after pre-registration. Severity strata for skill-by-severity reporting.
strata <- c(0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 1)
```

### Evaluation harness

Every metric and test named above was implemented below, before any label exists, so that when labels arrive the confirmatory analysis runs rather than being written. Nothing here reads outcome data; the functions take vectors and return numbers, and the chunk that follows exercises each one on inputs whose answers are known by construction.

```{r}
#| label: eval-harness
#| echo: true
#| output: false
# Recall at a fixed precision. The operating point is chosen on the calibration
# data and applied unchanged elsewhere, per the pre-registration: choosing it on
# the test fold would report the best threshold in hindsight.
threshold_at_precision <- function(score, positive, target = 0.90) {
  ord <- order(score, decreasing = TRUE)
  tp <- cumsum(positive[ord])
  prec <- tp / seq_along(tp)
  ok <- which(prec >= target & tp > 0)
  if (!length(ok)) return(Inf)          # target precision unreachable
  score[ord][max(ok)]
}
recall_at_threshold <- function(score, positive, thr) {
  if (!sum(positive)) return(NA_real_)
  if (!is.finite(thr)) return(0)
  sum(score >= thr & positive) / sum(positive)
}

# Confusion matrix with user's accuracy (correct / predicted as that class) and
# producer's accuracy (correct / reference of that class).
confusion <- function(truth, pred, lev = sort(unique(c(truth, pred)))) {
  m <- table(pred = factor(pred, lev), truth = factor(truth, lev))
  d <- diag(m)
  data.frame(class = lev,
             n_reference = as.integer(colSums(m)),
             n_predicted = as.integer(rowSums(m)),
             users = ifelse(rowSums(m) > 0, d / rowSums(m), NA_real_),
             producers = ifelse(colSums(m) > 0, d / colSums(m), NA_real_),
             row.names = NULL)
}

rmse <- function(obs, pred) sqrt(mean((pred - obs)^2))
mae <- function(obs, pred) mean(abs(pred - obs))
rrmse <- function(obs, pred) rmse(obs, pred) / mean(obs)

# Theil's U inequality coefficient with the bias, variance and covariance
# proportions of mean squared error, which sum to one by construction. The
# decomposition separates systematic offset from unexplained scatter.
theil <- function(obs, pred) {
  mse <- mean((pred - obs)^2)
  if (mse == 0) return(c(U = 0, bias = 0, variance = 0, covariance = 0))
  n <- length(obs)
  sd_p <- sqrt(mean((pred - mean(pred))^2))     # population sd, so the
  sd_o <- sqrt(mean((obs - mean(obs))^2))       # proportions sum to one
  r <- if (sd_p == 0 || sd_o == 0) 0 else cor(obs, pred)
  c(U = sqrt(mse) / (sqrt(mean(obs^2)) + sqrt(mean(pred^2))),
    bias = (mean(pred) - mean(obs))^2 / mse,
    variance = (sd_p - sd_o)^2 / mse,
    covariance = 2 * (1 - r) * sd_p * sd_o / mse)
}

# Paired fold-wise test: one-sided Wilcoxon signed rank on the per-fold
# difference, with a block bootstrap over folds for the interval. Resampling
# folds rather than cells is what keeps spatial dependence inside a resampling
# unit.
paired_fold_test <- function(diff, alternative = "greater", B = 10000,
                             seed = 20260812) {
  p <- suppressWarnings(wilcox.test(diff, alternative = alternative)$p.value)
  set.seed(seed)
  bs <- replicate(B, mean(sample(diff, length(diff), replace = TRUE)))
  c(mean_diff = mean(diff), p_value = p,
    ci_low = unname(quantile(bs, 0.025)),
    ci_high = unname(quantile(bs, 0.975)))
}

# McNemar on paired cell-level detections: only the discordant pairs carry
# information about which method is better.
mcnemar_paired <- function(correct_a, correct_b) {
  b <- sum(correct_a & !correct_b); c_ <- sum(!correct_a & correct_b)
  if (b + c_ == 0) return(c(b = 0, c = 0, p_value = 1))
  c(b = b, c = c_,
    p_value = suppressWarnings(
      mcnemar.test(matrix(c(sum(correct_a & correct_b), b, c_,
                            sum(!correct_a & !correct_b)), 2))$p.value))
}

# The detectability floor: the lowest severity stratum whose skill clears the
# pre-registered threshold. Strata must be supplied in ascending order.
detectability_floor <- function(stratum, skill, threshold = 0.50) {
  ok <- which(!is.na(skill) & skill >= threshold)
  if (!length(ok)) return(NA_character_)
  as.character(stratum[min(ok)])
}

# The three confirmatory tests form one family; Holm controls it.
holm_family <- function(p, labels) {
  data.frame(test = labels, p_raw = p,
             p_holm = p.adjust(p, method = "holm"), row.names = NULL)
}
```

The harness was exercised on constructed inputs whose correct answers follow from their construction rather than from running the code. A check that cannot fail proves nothing, so each case below has a determinate expected value and the chunk stops if any disagrees.

```{r}
#| label: eval-checks-data
#| echo: true
#| output: false
chk <- function(what, expected, got, tol = 1e-8)
  data.frame(check = what, expected = round(expected, 4),
             got = round(got, 4), passes = abs(expected - got) < tol)

# Perfectly separable scores: the 0.90-precision threshold recovers every
# positive, so recall is exactly 1.
s1 <- 10:1; p1 <- c(rep(TRUE, 5), rep(FALSE, 5))
r1 <- recall_at_threshold(s1, p1, threshold_at_precision(s1, p1, 0.90))

# Inverted scores: precision peaks at 0.5, never reaches 0.90, so the operating
# point does not exist and recall must be 0 rather than an accidental number.
p2 <- c(rep(FALSE, 5), rep(TRUE, 5))
r2 <- recall_at_threshold(s1, p2, threshold_at_precision(s1, p2, 0.90))

# A constant offset of 1: RMSE and MAE are 1, and relative RMSE is 1 / mean(obs).
o3 <- c(1, 2, 3); p3 <- o3 + 1

# Theil proportions sum to one for any non-degenerate pair, and U is 0 when
# prediction is exact.
t4 <- theil(c(0.1, 0.4, 0.2, 0.8), c(0.2, 0.3, 0.25, 0.9))
t5 <- theil(o3, o3)

# Pure bias: prediction is observation plus a constant, so all of the mean
# squared error is the bias term and none of it is variance or covariance.
t6 <- theil(o3, p3)

# Eight positive fold differences: the one-sided signed-rank p is 2^-8.
d7 <- seq(0.1, 0.8, by = 0.1)
w7 <- paired_fold_test(d7)

# Holm is never anti-conservative.
h8 <- holm_family(c(0.01, 0.02, 0.03), c("H1", "H2", "H3"))

# Skill clears 0.50 first in the third stratum.
f9 <- detectability_floor(c("0.01", "0.03", "0.05", "0.10"),
                          c(0.10, 0.20, 0.55, 0.70))

# A confusion matrix with one known error: class a is predicted for one true b,
# so user's accuracy for a is 2/3 and producer's accuracy for b is 1/2.
c10 <- confusion(c("a", "a", "b", "b"), c("a", "a", "a", "b"))

checks <- rbind(
  chk("recall at 0.90 precision, separable", 1, r1),
  chk("recall when 0.90 precision unreachable", 0, r2),
  chk("RMSE of a unit offset", 1, rmse(o3, p3)),
  chk("MAE of a unit offset", 1, mae(o3, p3)),
  chk("relative RMSE, mean 2", 0.5, rrmse(o3, p3)),
  chk("Theil proportions sum to one", 1, sum(t4[c("bias", "variance",
                                                  "covariance")])),
  chk("Theil U of an exact prediction", 0, t5[["U"]]),
  chk("pure offset is all bias", 1, t6[["bias"]]),
  chk("pure offset has no variance term", 0, t6[["variance"]]),
  chk("one-sided Wilcoxon on 8 positives", 2^-8, w7[["p_value"]], 1e-6),
  chk("bootstrap interval brackets the mean", 1,
      as.numeric(w7[["ci_low"]] <= mean(d7) && w7[["ci_high"]] >= mean(d7))),
  chk("Holm is not anti-conservative", 1,
      as.numeric(all(h8$p_holm >= h8$p_raw))),
  chk("detectability floor is the lowest clearing stratum", 0.05,
      as.numeric(f9)),
  chk("user's accuracy for class a", 2 / 3, c10$users[c10$class == "a"]),
  chk("producer's accuracy for class b", 0.5,
      c10$producers[c10$class == "b"]))

stopifnot(all(checks$passes))
```

All `r nrow(checks)` checks pass, which is the only reason the document renders past this point. Two of them are worth naming because they encode decisions rather than arithmetic. The second case builds scores in which no threshold reaches the required precision, and requires the harness to return zero recall rather than silently reporting the recall of whatever threshold came closest, which is how a fixed-precision metric is most easily misreported. The bootstrap case resamples folds rather than cells, so spatial dependence stays inside the resampling unit; resampling cells would treat neighbouring stands as independent and return an interval far too narrow.

```{r}
#| label: planned-baseline
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# post (2019-2021) summer means per stand cell, per Zwieback et al. (2024).
```

# Results

Values in this section populate when the pre-registered analysis executes; every table below is rendered from the analysis code with its final structure, and cells display as pending until model training completes. No value in this section is estimated, assumed or illustrative. The section is written in the present tense throughout, unlike the completed Methods sections, because the analyses it reports have not run and describing them in the past would assert work that has not happened. Each subsection states the decision rule its table will be read against, all of them fixed by pre-registration, so the reading is committed before the numbers arrive rather than fitted to them.

## Severity skill

@tbl-severity reports severity-estimation skill per severity stratum for the two deep learning models and the SWIR change baseline on identical stand cells, read down the strata rather than across the models, because the question is where skill fails rather than which model wins, and giving root-mean-square error, relative RMSE normalised by the stratum mean of the reference severity, mean absolute error, and Theil's U with its bias, variance and covariance proportions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-severity
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Severity estimation error per severity stratum and model, from block spatial cross-validation. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
strata_lab <- c("0-0.01", "0.01-0.03", "0.03-0.05", "0.05-0.10",
                "0.10-0.20", ">0.20")
models <- c("TempCNN", "Transformer", "SWIR baseline")
sev_shell <- expand.grid(Stratum = strata_lab, Model = models,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
sev_shell[c("RMSE", "rRMSE", "MAE", "U_Theil", "U_bias", "U_var", "U_cov")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(sev_shell, right = c("RMSE","rRMSE","MAE","U_Theil","U_bias","U_var","U_cov"))
```

## Detection skill

@tbl-detection reports the confusion-matrix summary per stratum, user's and producer's accuracy and the primary metric, recall at 0.90 precision, with fold-wise dispersion. The detectability floor of each method is read from this table as the lowest stratum whose recall at 0.90 precision reaches 0.50, a rule and a threshold both fixed before any outcome was seen, so the floor is located rather than chosen. Table S10 carries the H1 test, the fold-wise paired difference in the primary metric between each deep model and the baseline within the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, its block-bootstrap confidence interval, the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic, and the McNemar cell-level check. The detectability floor of each model is the lowest stratum whose primary metric exceeds the pre-registered threshold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-detection
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Detection skill per severity stratum and model, giving user's accuracy (UA), producer's accuracy (PA), and recall at 0.90 precision (R90, the pre-registered primary metric), with fold-wise standard deviation. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
det_shell <- expand.grid(Stratum = strata_lab, Model = models,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
det_shell[c("UA", "PA", "R90", "R90_sd")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(det_shell, right = c("UA","PA","R90","R90_sd"))
```

## Onset dating

@tbl-onset reports onset-year error under the two supervision regimes, testing H2, and gives mean absolute error and root-mean-square error in years, the share of predictions falling within the label bracket, and the fold-wise paired difference between triangulated and single-epoch supervision. The share falling inside the bracket is the more informative column, because mean absolute error against a bracketed truth penalises a prediction that is correct in every sense the labels can express.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-onset
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Onset-year estimation error by model and supervision regime (triangulated two-epoch intervals against single-epoch labels), with the H2 paired test. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
onset_shell <- expand.grid(Model = c("TempCNN", "Transformer"),
                           Supervision = c("Triangulated", "Single-epoch"),
                           KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
onset_shell[c("MAE_yr", "RMSE_yr", "In_bracket", "Delta_MAE", "Wilcoxon_p")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(onset_shell, right = c("MAE_yr","RMSE_yr","In_bracket","Delta_MAE","Wilcoxon_p"))
```

## Climate contribution

@tbl-climate reports H3 as fold-wise paired differences in the primary detection metric and in onset error between climate-augmented and spectral-only models. The pairing is what carries the test, since the two arms differ in their input channels alone and are trained on identical folds, so a difference cannot be attributed to the split. All three confirmatory tests belong to one family and are corrected together by the Holm procedure, which means each is read at its corrected level rather than at 0.05.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-climate
#| echo: true
#| tbl-cap: "Test of H3, climate-augmented against spectral-only models, fold-wise paired differences with Holm-corrected one-sided Wilcoxon tests. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
h3_shell <- data.frame(Model = c("TempCNN", "Transformer"),
                       Delta_R90 = "pending", Delta_MAE_yr = "pending",
                       CI95 = "pending", Wilcoxon_p = "pending")
fmt_tbl(h3_shell, right = c("Delta_R90", "Delta_MAE_yr", "CI95", "Wilcoxon_p"))
```

## Independent evaluation

Table S11 reports agreement with the untouched severity reference of @Zwieback_2024 in the Talkeetna to Byers Lake footprint, using only fold models whose training excluded the footprint, and carries the same error slate as @tbl-severity at 90 m and 30 m support, alongside the published within-study errors of the reference itself for context, which are not directly comparable and are marked as such.

## Outbreak progression

Table S12 compares reconstructed annual outbreak area against the aerial survey record, reported as descriptive correspondence, giving mapped area, surveyed area, their ratio, and the intersection-over-union of the footprints per year.

# Discussion

## Detection floor

[Pending: interpretation of @tbl-severity, @tbl-detection and Table S10.] The decisive comparison is confined to the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, where @Zwieback_2024 found stand-scale SWIR change uninformative and where roughly ninety percent of the region's beetle-killed spruce resides. If Table S10 shows the radar models clearing the published floor within that stratum, the detectability floor of freely available imagery drops below the published 0.1 threshold and the fraction of the outbreak visible to open-data monitoring rises accordingly; if it does not, the result consolidates the case that sub-metre imagery is a hard requirement for low-severity beetle mapping in mixed boreal forest, itself a finding with operational cost implications, and one already implied by the resolution comparison @Hart_2015 ran on this same beetle. Either outcome resolves the transfer question left open between the defoliator system of @Perbet_2024, where temporal deep learning recovered partial disturbance from Landsat, and the bark beetle system here, whose multi-year fade [@Hicke_2024; @Kautz_2024] presents a slower but weaker annual signal.

## Temporal supervision

[Pending: interpretation of @tbl-onset.] The triangulation design tests a claim with reach beyond this outbreak, that a second high-resolution label epoch buys more onset-dating skill than any refinement of a single-epoch label set, because it converts static labels into interval-censored ones and exposes annotation errors through cross-epoch consistency. The expected one to two year lag between spectral change and onset [@Perbet_2024] bounded what an annual optical method could date; the monthly radar record makes the censoring bracket finer without changing the loss, and @tbl-onset quantifies how much of that bound the interval supervision recovers. Dating from daily commercial imagery narrows that bound at a price this study is designed to avoid [@Nowak_2026], so the comparison worth making is not against the best achievable dating but against what open data alone can date. The four-cut footprint, where the labels of @Zwieback_2024 interleave with both mosaic epochs, indicates the ceiling available where label epochs are dense.

## Limitations

Seven limitations are known by design. First, crown labels derive from visual interpretation of sub-metre imagery, so fully occluded dead spruce under closed deciduous canopy are absent from both training and reference data, and severity is accordingly a minimum estimate in dense mixed stands [@Zwieback_2024]. Second, the dual-polarisation radar record over this frame begins in June 2017, after the outbreak began, so there is no pre-outbreak radar state and no change from one; the models recognise a trajectory rather than a departure, and stands that died before the record opened carry an open bracket rather than an onset. Third, the frozen season moves C-band backscatter further than any canopy loss does, since freezing took more than 3 dB out of the ERS-1 return from a black spruce stand near Manley Hot Springs between day of year 270 and 290 [@Rignot_1994] where total canopy removal by windthrow moved the mean by 0.45 dB in VV and 0.68 dB in VH [@R_etschi_2019], so the monthly series carries a seasonal cycle larger than its signal and the models must either work within season or learn the freeze state, which no standard for boreal forest radar specifies. Fourth, no layover and shadow mask was applied to the radar record, and thermal noise removal, which published processing graphs place first, is not mentioned in the terrain corrected product's description and has not been verified here; the offset against the independent mosaic being larger in the weaker polarisation is consistent with residual noise and is a hypothesis with a stated test rather than a finding. Fifth, the independent severity reference is itself a model product with documented error structure, not ground truth; agreement with it bounds, rather than establishes, map accuracy. Sixth, mortality agent is inferred from context, not confirmed by ground observation, and other agents of spruce death are conflated with beetle kill at unknown but presumed low rates, a conflation that separating agents by their spectral and temporal signatures is the established way to attack [@Meigs_2011; @Senf_2015]. Seventh, the study area is one outbreak in one region; transfer to the Kenai Peninsula, to Interior Alaska or to other *Dendroctonus* systems is untested and, on the evidence of cross-system transfer failures elsewhere [@Kautz_2024], should not be presumed, and the outbreak that has been studied most closely in a comparable system was governed by summer, winter and multi-year drought, indexed there by low peak snow water equivalent, none of which the three temperature channels used here carry [@Hart_2017].

## Operational implications

\[Pending: contingent on Tables S10 and S12.\] The aerial detection survey remains the only annual statewide observation system, and nothing here replaces it; the question is what a free satellite complement adds. A model whose floor sits below 0.1 severity would flag dispersed mortality the surveys under-record, at monthly cadence, through cloud, over unflown terrain, for the cost of compute alone, with the reconstructed progression in Table S12 indicating how faithfully such a system would have tracked this outbreak had it run from 2016. The label pipeline is the transferable asset, since statewide sub-metre mosaics now recur, and each new epoch extends the interval-censored label set without new fieldwork. That is the same argument the survey programme reviews reach from the opposite direction, that remote sensing augments a survey whose consistency and coverage cannot scale to a continental forest estate [@Hall_2016; @Housman_2018], and it is the direction the record of insect disturbance has already taken elsewhere, where an annual national series now runs from 1985 [@White_2017; @Perbet_2025].

# Conclusion

\[Pending: quantitative sentences follow the pre-registered analysis.\] This study asks a bounded question with a decade of consequence behind it, how much of a spruce beetle outbreak freely available satellite data can see. Prior work fixed the answer at severities above 0.1 [@Zwieback_2024], leaving most beetle-killed trees in this landscape invisible to open-data monitoring, and the wider literature on bark beetle detection has concentrated on the earliest and the most severe stages rather than on the dispersed middle [@Marvasti_Zadeh_2023; @Morris_2016]. The design assembled here tests whether temporal deep learning moves that boundary, using only open data end to end, a terrain-corrected Sentinel-1 radar series filtered across its own length, crown labels digitised on public statewide mosaics, onset intervals triangulated between mosaic epochs, and an independent published severity product as referee. Whatever the direction of the result, the study delivers the first annually resolved, openly reproducible record of the 2016 to 2025 Southcentral Alaska outbreak at stand scale, a labelled dataset positioned to grow with each statewide mosaic epoch, and a pre-registered benchmark against which subsequent methods, sensors and regions can be measured.

# Data availability

All inputs are publicly retrievable; the download script, checksums and provenance manifest are in the project repository. The severity rasters of @Zwieback_2024 are archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.8423568, the crown labels at doi:10.5281/zenodo.10569990 and the trained network at doi:10.5281/zenodo.10569975; the latter two are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, while the severity rasters carry no declared licence and are used for independent evaluation only, pending clarification with the author. Aerial detection survey data are distributed by the United States Forest Service as public-domain works, and Sentinel-2, Landsat and elevation data are open under their respective public licences. The Maxar mosaics of the State of Alaska Geoportal are accessible for non-commercial use by streaming, and their pixels are processed locally and never redistributed; what this study publishes from them is derived crowns and severity fractions, on the same footing as the published delineations it started from.

This study's own derived outputs are committed with the manuscript rather than deposited separately, because each is small and each is read at render time by the code that reports it. The literature screening table, the block sample with its fold assignment, and the annual and monthly climate series are under `02.inputs/derived`; the crown network's per-epoch metrics, the operating-point sweep, the triage queue, the endmember calibration, the synthetic validation summaries, the per-block annual reflectance trajectories and the per-cell clear-observation record are under `03.outputs`. Every number in the text is read from one of those files at render time, so the manuscript cannot report a figure the committed data does not contain.
